summary: The respondent assessee was assessed to wealth tax for the assessment years 1965 66, 1966 67 and 1967 68 on cash basis. The Wealth Tax Officer included a sum of Rs.3,37,497/ as his net wealth in the status of a Hindu Undivided Family. In each of the assessments, the Wealth Tax officer included a sums of Rs,3,38,496/ as interest due on accrual basis. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that interest accrued to the assessee on the money lending investments could not be included in the wealth tax assessment of the assessee. The Appellate Tribunal confirmed this view and held that the interest accrued was liable to be included under the wealth Tax assessments of the assesee. In the appeals before this Court it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that interest was liable for be included, in the net wealth of the assesses. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The computation of the net assets of an assessee calls for a determination of his assets and debts as on the valuation date. All the assets of the assessees bar those expressly excepted by the statute, are to be taken into account, and it is immaterial whether the assessee employs one system of accounting or another. There is clear indication that the assets to be considered are not circumscribed by any consideration of the particular system of accountancy adopted by the assessee.[310B C] 2. The method of accounting, mercantile, mercantile or cash or hybrid, is of no relevance for the purpose of determining the assets. That being so, the conclusion is inescapable that even though the accounts of theassessee are maintained on cash and basis, though not realised, on the outstandings of the money lent business are liable to he included in net wealth. [310C D] 3. The system of mercantile accounting, or mercantile, cash or Hybrid is of relevance for determining the asset of an assesee under the Wealth tax Act. That is plainly from the definition or "net wealth" which speaks of "the aggregate value of all the assets" belonging to the assesees on the value date. [311D E] 4.

The respondent was a civilian employee of the appellant. He was dismissed from service by an order dated 9th October, 1987. The appel lant challenged his dismissal before the Central Administrative Tribunal which held that the penalty imposed upon him was not justified and directed reinstatement in service with back wages. The Tribunal also held that there had been violation of the rules of natural justice. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court which was dismissed by the learned Single Judge. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1. In the case of transfer proceedings to the Tribu nal, the Tribunal can exercise all the powers whi ch the civil court could in a suit or the High Courts in a proceeding could have exercised. It would be open to the Govern ment to decide whether on the basis of the charges, the punishment of dismissal should be maintain ed or else whether a lesser penalty would suffice. [33G H] 2.2. The power under Rule 16(1) of the Central Civil Services (Classification, Control and Appeal) Rules, 1965 is not absolute in its terms. It is open to an authority to impose any penalty which he may consider necessary for the purpose of imposing it. If the penalty is imposed without complying with the rules, it would be a case of no penalty. [34B] 3.1 The power conferred on the Governmen t servant under Rule 17(1), is not conditional upon the imposition of a lesser punishment. It does not depend upon the nature and extent of the penalty to which the delinquent is liable. The Court can impose only such penalty as it thinks fit. If it is found that the respondent was not in fact the person convicted, it must consider whether the charge alone would have weighed with the authority in imposing the punishment. [35F] 2:2. In order to decide on whether a higher penalty should be maintained or else, whether a greater penalty would be sufficient, the Court has to consider whether there is some evidence even if some of it is find that he was not likely to have offi cial dealings with the respondent. If there is no such evidence, the court may interfere with the penalty if the conclusion of the Inquiry Officer or the Tribunal prima facie makes out a case for misdemeanour. [36F] 3:3. The High Court has not gone into the question whether the findings of the inquiry officer or the Tribun al are vitiated by any finding as to substantial misdemeanour for which the punishment can be lawfully imposed. If, however, the conclusion is that the delinquent was a person likely to ha ve been offi ble, it is not for the Court to consider what would have weigh ed with the authori ty in imposing such penalty.

The appellants are the legal representatives of Respondent No.1 who died pendente lite and were in possession of certain properties. The first respondent filed a suit for declaration and an injunction to restrain the appellants from dispossessing him from the property known as 'Palmar Oit doeral Predio Aivao ' or 'Pedio Aus ' or Pedio ' or any other suitable place. The appellants contended that the suit was barred by Order 2 Rule 2(3) of the Code of Civil Procedure and had, therefore, been rightly dismissed as the Trial Court came to the conclusion that the plaintiff was no more in possession. The High Court dismissed the second appeal holding that the subsequent suit based on a distinct cause of action not found in the former suit and hence it did not lie. In this appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellants that the earlier suit based upon the factum of tenancy was not maintainable. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The jurisdiction of the civil court is specifically barred by order 2 Rule2(3). [1032E] 1.2 The jurisdiction is vested in the Mamlatdar under section 7 of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948. Section 58(2) bars the jurisdiction of all other courts to settle, decide or deal with any question which is by or under the Act required to be settled, decided or dealt with by any patent authority to settle. [1033G] 1:3 The jurisdiction vested in a civil court stands wholly barred by virtue of section 58(1) read with section 58 (2). In such a situation the Civil Court would not be competent to pass any order for restoration of possession to the deemed tenant. [1132B C] 1 :4 The jurisdiction, therefore. vested in Mamlatdar under Section 7 of Bombay Tenancy & Agricultural Lands act 1948 is, therefore,. vested in him under section 8(2). [1133G H] 1(a) In the instant case, the appellants had not applied to the Mamlatdar for possession of the land within the period allowed by Section 18 of the Act and had therefore, allowed the first respondent to become a deemed purchaser of the suit property on the strength of his tenancy. The jurisdiction was, therefore vested in Civil Court under section 58 of the Tenancy Act. [1233G; 1034A] (b) In view of the decision of this Court in the case of K.K. Jain vs M/s. K.M. Jain & Co., ; , the civil suit was based on the factum that the tenancy was in the manner authorised by Section 9. The Civil Court had no jurisdiction to entertain the suit. [934B C; 1035A] 2:1 The High Courts have taken the view that even after the Fifth Amendment came into force, the plaintiff had not apply to the Tehsildar for possession within the time allowed by section 18 of Act and therefore, had allowed the defendant to become deemed purchaser. [833C D] 2.2 In such circumstances, the Civil court would be entitled to deal with the dispute on the footing that the defendant was a trespasser.

The petitioners are carpenters in the Himachal Pradesh State Handicrafts Corporation. They claim that they are being paid the same wages as are payable to carpenter, painters and carpents, painter and carpenterers. The Corporation has adopted the minimum wages payable for similar work in the construction industry. The petitioners have claimed that they were entitled to "equal pay for equal work" as carpentors or in the alternative, the minimum wage prescribed by the Deputy Commissioner for like categories of workmen. They also claim that the Corporation has not fixed the mini mum wages payable to the carpentes, paints and carpents. The respondents have filed a counter affidavit stating that there are no regular employees of the petitioners ' establishment and as such, the question of payment to the petitioners, the same pay admissible to regular employees does not arise. It is also stated that the petitioners are doing carpenter and carpentryers in Government service. The respondent Corporation has stated that there were no regular workers of the petitioner 's categories in its establishment and, as such the question cannot be enforced. Disposing of the petition, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The principle of "equal wages for equal pay" cannot be invoked invariably in every kind of service particularly in the area of professional services. [667B] 2.1 In the instant case, the petitioners were employed by a company incorporated under the . By the general description of their job, one cannot come to the conclusion that every carpenter or craftsman is equal to the other in the performance of his work. The principle has to be read into Article 14 of the Constitution. [669C D] 2:2. In the first place even assum ing that the petitioner are doing tailoring and carpering work, there may be qualitative difference as regards reliability and responsibility. One cannot deny that often the difference is a matter of degree and that there is an element of value judgment by those who are charged with the administration in fixing the scales of pay and other conditions of service. [670D E] 2 :3. The principal claim of the peti tioners is not one of the fundamental rights expressly guaranteed by our Constitution. Unless it is shown that there was a discrimination amongst the same set of employees by the same master in the same establishment, the principle of equal pay for Equal work cannot be implemented invariably in each kind of serv ice. [671F] 4:4. The principles of " Equal pay forequal work" cannot he enforced. They are being denied equal pay on par with their counterparts in Government serv ice, the petitioner cannot enforce the right to " equal pay".

The prosecution case against the appellants was that on the night of 10th October 1975, when P.W. 2 and his wife were returning home from their fields, all the accused armed with deadly weapons entered into a conspiracy to commit murder of her husband and in furtherance thereof they committed the murder of his wife. The deceased was also charged under section 302 read with section 34 I.P.C. for having committed the offence of murder of the wife. It was contended on behalf of the appellants that the retracted confession of accused 5 could not be relied upon against him as he had been acquitted by the High Court and also by the fact that accused 6 had been convicted along with accused 1, 2 and 6 for the murder and the conviction of accused 7 under section 120B I. P.C., was bad in law. The High Court rejected the contention of the State that the confession of the accused 5 was not a party to the conspiracy and that he had also been acquitted. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the High court 's judgment confirming his conviction and sentence awarded to him by the trial court under section 27 read with s 120B, I.C.; was bad as the retracted confessional confession of appellant 5 could be relied on against him in view of the fact he had not been acquitted at all; that the evidence of P.Ws. 2, 3, 4 and 7 who were eye witnesses to the occurrence was highly interested and partisan and that they had acted in a most unfair manner in implicating the appellants. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The retracted confession made by accused 5 cannot be relied against him. [782 B] 2. The evidence of PWs. 2 to 3 clearly established the conspiracy between the two groups. It is not possible to accept their testimony that they were interested and that the deceased was a party thereto. They had acted as a result of the conspiracy. There is no reason why they should be excluded from consideration for convicting them under section 34, I P. C. [783 D] 3. The confession made in this case could not have been relied upon by the prosecution against the other accused persons. It cannot be said that the appellants were prejudiced because of their acquittal by the Sessions Judge. [784 E F] 4. The Court has to see whether the retracted confessions are true and reliable. If they are accepted, it is for the court to consider whether they are true or not. [781 G H] 5. In the instant case, the High Courts have found that the prosecution had failed to prove the conspiracy beyond all reasonable doubt and that there was no evidence to show that the accused 6 who were involved in the conspiracy had committed the crime of murder. The appellants were rightly convicted under section 304B IP. C., read with sections 34 I P .C. [780 G H; 781 A] 6. The prosecution has failed to establish that the appellant 1 and 2 formed part of the unlawful assembly, that they formed an unlawful assembly in furtherance of their common intention and in pursuance thereof they acted in furtherance or in furtherance and that in furtherance 'of their common object they committed murder of their wife. [779 C D] 7. The mere fact that the other two groups were members of the same group cannot be a ground to reject their testimony. It would not be correct to say that the two independent witnesses were interested in the actual occurrence. There was no reason for them to falsely implicate the appellants in this crime. [777 E F; 781 B] 8. The fact that one of the groups was not present at the scene of occurrence and the other group was not examined by the eye witnesses cannot be taken into consideration as a ground for convicting the appellants under section302 read with 34 IP .C., because, there is no evidence on record to show any overt act or intention of the other members of that group. [78 E F G] 9.

The appellant was the sole executor of a will alleged to have been executed by Lakshmamma in favour of the respondent. The question for decision in this appeal was whether the will set up by him was not proved to be the last will and testament of Lakshmammal. Held, that the evidence of the attesting witnesses on the execution of the will was highly improbable and the High Court had rightly held that the will in question was not established. The onus of proving the signature of the testatrix on the propounder was heavy on him and it was incumbent upon him to prove that the testator was in a sound disposing state of mind or that he understood the nature and effect of its contents. Held further, that there was no evidence about the execution by the appellant of the Will which would show that the testatrix had really understood its contents and the effect of the dispositions made before her signature. The High Court was right in holding that on proof of the signature on the will the propounder could not be held to have proved that the executant fully understood the contents of the document and put his signature on it when she was in sound disposing State of mind. Held also, further,that the evidence about execution by itself did not establish that the propounder had really known the contents thereof and put her signatures on it before he put her signature to the will. The mere fact that the attesting witness had signed the will would not make him a suspicious circumstance. The evidence of this witness is clearly inconsistent with the appellant 's case about previous instructions and so it would be difficult to treat the evidence as suffi cient to prove the execution.

The appellant company was registered under the Andhra Pradesh General Sales Tax Act, 1957. The sales tax authorities assessed the turnover of the appellant company for two assessment years 1965 66 and 1966 77 on the ground that they fall under entry No. 4 of the 1st Schedule to the Act. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the assessing authority but the Tribunal allowed an appeal holding that the carbons were covered by Entry 41 of the First Schedule to that Act. In reference, the High Court held that the motor vehicles manufactured by the appellant were rightly subjected to sales tax for two years 1965 67 and 1966 78 on the view that they fell under entry 18 of the first schedule to the Andhra Act. Dismissing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: The High Court correctly held that carbonons are covered by the relevant entry 4 of Schedule 1 of the Madras General Sales tax Act, 1939. [562 D] The word "assets" is used in the schedule to describe goods which may have been manufactured for use as an aid or addition. It will be noticed that the term "accessories" is employed in the Schedule to describe Goods which may be manufactured for purposes of equipment or accessories connected with the main purpose. [563 E] The expression "electrical goods" is defined in section 2(g) of the Act to mean "a material used in relation to any process, whether manual or otherwise, for use in connection with, or incidental to, the execution of a contract". The word 'assets ' has been used in several entries including parts. [564 G] The term "electric goods" in entry No 4 of 1st schedule refers to "all kinds of articles by putting in the words "not being such articles as are ordinarily also used for other purposes", and excludes certain other articles by put in the said entry merely because a purchaser makes some other use of it.

The petitioners in these petitions challenged the validity of a notification issued by the Government of Gujarat on June 26, 1985 amending the Gujarat Minor Mineral Rules 1966 substituting the original rule 21 as Rule 21. The petitioners contended that under Entry 50 of List II of 7th Schedule to the Constitution, the royalty recovered by the State Government had to be used only for mineral development and could not be used for any other purpose; that the impugned notification in question was in contravention of clause (b) of Article 304 of the Constitution inasmuch as it purported to levy royalty on minor minerals at the rate of 50 per cent of the royalty payable by the lessees and no royalty was payable by village potters who manufacture upto one lakh bricks per year and by the village potter whose annual production was not exceeding two lakh bricks and which supply at least one lakh brick and which supplies at least two lakh brick, which supply in more than one lakh, bricks to the Rural Housing Board or Panchayats; that under Rule 21 a holder of a Parwana granted under the Rules has to pay royalty at the rates specified in column 2 of the said Schedule; and that no royalty shall be charged from any owner, employee, contractor or sub lessee from the leased area at the scales specified in columns 3 of the Schedule. The State Government issued a notification on June 27, 1985 substituting the old rule 21 with effect from January 1, 1985. The original rule 22 was substituted by new rule 21 which provided that a holder or a quarry lease or any other mineral concession granted under any rule made under sub section (1) of Section 15 of the Act shall pay royalty in respect of minor minerals provided in column 3 of Schedule. In exercise of its powers conferred by section 15 of , the State of Gujarat issued a Notification dated June 26 1985 substituting Rule 21 as amended by the new rule 22. The petitioner in some of the petitions had two contentions: (1 ) that under entry 50 of the 7th schedule to the Act, royalty recovered from the lessee was being treated as part of the consolidated fund of the State and used for other purposes by the respondent State; and (2) that the levy was bad because the said royalty was being regarded as part and parcel of the Consolidated Fund of the state. Dismissing the petitions, ^ HELD: 1. The impugned notification dated June 27 1985 substituted Rule 21 with retrospective effect from February 1,1985. [408C] 2.1 The State Legislature has not delegated its power to the State Legislature to make a law for regulating the grant of quarry leases or other mineral concessions in re spect of minor mineral and for purposes connected therewith. The Act is passed for devel opment of minerals but while discharging its functions relating to development, if the State incidentally allows mining to be carried on in the public interest and levies in that connection a tax, it does not mean that the said tax should be used merely for development of minerals and not for other purpose sanctioned by law. [414D E] 2(a) The Act has been passed for the benefit of the weaker sections of society and if under rule 21 a concession is shown in their favour it cannot be said that there is no reasonable nexus between the classification for purposes of the proviso to Rule 21 to show concession in the matter of payment of royalty and the social policy underlying the Constitution. [416E] 2.(b) The State incidentally permits mining to he carried on by the lessee or sub lessees from the lease area at rates specified against them in column 1 of the schedule. The fact that section 15 authorises the State Gov ernment to show such concession while promulgating the Rules which are in the nature of subordi nate legislation is also of no consequence. [413F] 2 (c) The provisions of the Gujarat minor Mineral Rules, 1966 and the Rules made thereunder do not authorise the State Govern ment to make any classification for purpose of implementing the policy of the Rules under which the Rules are made.

The appellant was the trustee of a temple. He filed a suit for declaration that he was hereditary trustees and for possession of the property. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court reversed it holding that the appellant was not hereditary. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The definition of hereditary trustee in section 6(9) of Madras Act 19 of 1951 is identical in both the Acts. [426 B] (2) A hereditary trustee is in the nature of property. He is appointed by the founder and he has no right to hold office as a matter of course. He must be held to be a trustee within the meaning of section 6 (9). The artificial definition of "regulated" in section 2(9)(a) of Act 19, 1951, is identical with that of section 5(1) of the Madras Act 22 of 1959. [427 C] (3) A Hindu temple is not an hereditary one and it is a place of worship which is regulated by usage or custom. The word "regulated ' in section 4(9), therefore, means "to be granted by the trustee himself". It is well established that the office of a hereditary trustee must be transmitted to the successor according to some definite rules of descent by which his own force designate the person to succeed. [409 D E] (4) The artificial definitions of hereditary trustees in section 5 (9) are not exhaustive and do not apply where the ordinary rules of succession under the Hindu law are modified by usage and succession has to be determined in accordance with the modified rules.

The appellant was charged with murder and sentenced to death. The prosecution case against him was that on April 26, 1971 at about 10 p.m. he along with his brother (PW 4) went to the house of PW 4 where he was sleeping and saw the deceased going out of the cattle shed in the open space, which is shown in the site plan (exhibit P15), at No. 5, when they were sleeping on a bench outside his cattle shed. The appellant was seen sitting on a table outside his house while PW 4 was sleeping on the eastern side of the sluice. He ran away after the assault. The deceased was sleeping with him and he ran to his younger brother 's place where he fell down on the southern side of his cattle sheds. The other two accused were also sleeping on that bench. The trial court acquitted all the accused except one who was on the same boat with the appellant. In appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellant that the High Court had not considered the intrinsic quality of the evidence of PW4 and that he could not be convicted solely on the sole testimony of a single witness. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court has not considered its intrinsic quality as an absolutely reliable witness. It is also conceivable that those persons who arrived at the place of occurrence when he came running away after assault are likely to have escaped. [707 D] 2. In the instant case, there was a mention about a pool of blood only where the dead body was found at No 1 and there were no other witnesses to support the prosecution version. The evidence of PWs 1, 2 and 3 is corroborated by the contents of the FIR. The fact that PW 4 had stated in the first information report that 'my elder brother 'meaning the deceased was "chasing him from behind" in court he has completely given a go by to this statement and stated that when PW 4 came to the place where the occurrence took place, he saw the other assailants who were present there. The very fact that the witness has stated in his earlier version in the FIR stands contradicted by the testimony in Court on a very material point. [807 E F] 3. It may not be possible to adopt that course in this case where the testimony of PW 1 is to be believed, the crowd had gathered at the scene of occurrence already when he arrived. The witness may have seen some persons who would not ask him as to how it had happened. But the fact that he has stated the first Information Report that 'his elder brother"meaning him from inside his cattle farm was "solely given a went by this statement, for information with regard to the assailants. [777 G H] 4. The testimony of PWs I, 2 & 3 is not even credible and it is difficult to appreciate why they should be believed. PW 4 who arrived on the spot when he went near his deceased elder brother about hundred persons and there are some persons present there in a little later than PW 4. [779 A B] 5.

The respondents were the heirs and legal representatives of Amarchand who died in 1947. The Income tax Officer assessed the total income of the deceased Amarchand under section 24B(1) read with section 24 B of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, but no return was made within the period specified by the fiction incorporated in sub sections 1, 2 and 3 of section 24A. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the assessment order but the Tribunal held that the income which was received subsequent to the previous year could not be assessed as income received by Amarchand after his death. On reference the High Court answered the question against the Revenue. Held: (i) Under section 24(1), a person is liable to pay out of the estate of the person who dies before the assessment but the income was received by his heirs and representatives after his lifetime, they are liable for payment of the tax just as the deceased would have been liable when the income had not been assessed but would have become liable when he died. (ii) Under sub section (1), where a person dies in the previous years, the heirs or legal representatives are liable to be taxed in the hands of their heirs and heirs and the Income tax officer is entitled to assess the total Income of the said person as if the income were received by the deceased person before his death but in that previous year. (iii) Under the fiction created by section 24, a person becomes liable to tax under section 23B(2), even though he had not died before the date on which the Act came into force. The legal representatives who could be deemed to be assessees for the purpose of assessment in regard to those years were not liable to income tax in the several years of assessment. (iv) Under s 24B, the legal representatives have the right to assess their total income as if they had not expired and to claim that they are entitled to be assessed under section 22B(3). The legal representative has a right to make an application for being taxed under section 34B(4), but he is not liable for tax in those years. (v) Under cl. (b) of sub section 1, where the liability to pay income tax arises by reason of death or retirement of any person and the provisions of section 23A are mandatory, the proviso to that sub section applies only to cases where there has been a failure to pay the tax due under the Act. The fiction is limited to the cases provided in the three subsections of section24B and cannot be extended beyond the object for which it was enacted. (vi) Under el. (c), where an assessee dies before his retirement but the Income Tax Officer finds incorrect or incomplete then the Incometax Officer can make assessment on the total profits of the assessee as if he had died. The expression "accrue" in sub section(1)(b) is wide enough to include within its ambit all cases which are not covered by the proviso and are liable under the proviso. (vii) Under cls. (a), (b), (c) and (d), where the income is received by a person, if the Income 'tax Officer finds that incorrect or unclu sively the IncomeTax Officer has reason to believe that the assessee had not received the income, he may assess it as if it were an income of which he had received the salary. The word "accrued" in cl.(b) must be construed in its popular sense and not in a narrow or pedantic sense. (viii) Under clause (c)(i), where there is no express provision in the Act for the payment of tax, the liability of the heirs to pay tax arises only if the death has occurred before the last day of the previous month. The words "accumulated" and "accompanied by" are not intended to be restricted to cases which have been held not to be liable to assessment in the subsequent year.

The petitioners who were members of the Andhra Pradesh State Legislative Assembly, challenged the constitutional validity of the provisions of the Act on the ground that they contravened articles 14 and 16(1) (f), 19(1)(g) and 31 of the Constitution. The petitioners contended that the Act was ultra vires the Constitution as it violated article 14 inasmuch as it infringed articles 14, 19(i)(g). Held: (i) Article 16(3) is not a law providing for residence within the State or Union territory prior to its appointment or employment but only provides that the conditions of service applicable to members of a State shall be such as may be prescribed by the Central Government. The expression 'in relation to 'State ' has been substituted in article 372(2). The word 'State" has been used in the widest possible sense and includes within its ambit all persons who have been appointed either directly or by transfer to any office under the State. The word "State" is not defined in the Constitution but it is used in a wide sense as including within its fold every person who has been appointed, directly or indirectly, by transfer or appointment to an office under a State. (ii) Article 35(a) of the Constitu tion provides that nothing in article 16 shall prevent Parliament from making any law prescribing a requirement as to residence in a part of a state. The words 'in respect of any employment or appointment ' in article 35(b) are wide enough to include within its sweep all persons belonging to the same class or category and those who have not been appointed directly by transfer, appointment or appointment. (iii) Article 31(2) is an exception to article 16(i). The words "in relation" in article 31(1), therefore, must be given their ordinary meaning and must be construed as including all persons similarly situated. (iv) The word `State ' in the context of article 35 includes within it all persons whether belonging to a class or not. (v) The expression "any requirement as aforesaid" in cl. (2) of article 31 means that the person who is appointed, has been given an opportunity to make his representation against the proposed action and also to make representations against the action taken by him. (vi) The words `in relation ' in cl.(3) of Article 31 mean only those persons who are appointed directly or through a process of selection or appointment and not those who are already employed in connection with the affairs of the Union or State. If it chose to speak of residence in parts of the State as such, the Constitution would have provided for residence in the part of the state. (vii) The provisions of article 16 (1) do not apply to a case where the impugned Act is ultra vires on the grounds that they are inconsistent with articles 14 or 16(2), and that the impugned legislation is beyond the legislative competence of the Parliament.

The appellant was a postman attached to the Bulandshahr post office. He was tried for offences under sections 467 and 471 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860, and in two of them also for offences tinder sections 467, 471 and 471 Of the Indian penal Code. The trial court acquitted him but on appeal the High Court convicted him under section 52 of the Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the prosecution had merely shown that the registered letters were recovered from an almirah in the house in which the appellant lives jointly with his father and that the almirah contained a large number of articles belonging to the father, and since he had the key with him it must be deemed to be in possession of the almirah and consequently the presumption under section 54 of the Code of Criminal Procedure was not rebutted; (ii) the High court had wrongly assumed that the appellant was in exclusive possession of these articles for an inordinate length of time and had therefore no significance; (iii) the trial court had erred in holding that though the appellant 's father was in possession exclusively or even jointly with him, he could be said to have secreted them from the mere fact that they were found in the almirah which was said to be his exclusive possession. HELD : (i). The prosecution has failed to prove that these letters were in the exclusive possession and not merely in their joint possession. [419 C] (ii).The presumption under s 54 of 'the Code of Civil Procedure is a rebuttable one and must be strictly construed. It is only when the accused establishes his case by evidence that he was in actual possession of those articles or that he had no animus to possess them. The presumption under the section is not a rebuttable but it is only an exception to the general rule that where the burden of proof is upon the prosecution, the burden shifts on the accused to prove affirmatively that he has been in exclusive and exclusive possession with respect to the articles. [414 D E] (iii).The appellant had an opportunity to get at the articles and then infer that he must be presumed to bein possession along with his son because he had not the key of him with him. The fact that the keys were found by the father in the appellant did not make any difference.

The appellant was convicted by the trial court under section 409 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to pay a fine of Rs. 1,000/ . The High Court confirmed the conviction but reduced the sentence to one year 's rigorous imprisonment for two weeks. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the High Court had committed an error in interfering with the order of the trial judge. HELD : (i) The High court did not appreciate that the so called affidavit which was filed before the Panchas was in fact not an affidavit at all. It had not been sworn to before any person authorised to administer oaths. [117 B C] (ii) The appellant 's affidavit was not sworn to by any person appointed to administer it. It was no part of the duty of the Panches to enquire from the S.D.M. about the filing of the application before him. [119 D E] (iii) The order of conviction and sentence were based on a wrong assumption that the affidavit was filed after the proceedings had commenced and evidence taken. It is not possible for this Court to reappreciate the facts, but it would be desirable to interfere with the judgment of the High court in appeal if there is unimpeachable evidence that the judicial officer had knowledge of the order passed by him deliberately to pass the order. [118 E F] (iv) The fact that the appellant did not file an affidavit before the Panchayat was not an indication that he had actually made the affidavit. It would be a serious matter and a High Court should be chary finding of a judicial officer guilty of contempt of court.

The appellant was charged with murder and sentenced to death. The Sessions judge convicted him under section 302, I.P.C., but acquitted him on the ground that he had caused the death of Sheo Sahai. On appeal by special leave, Held, that the High Court erred in rejecting the statement of Ujagar Singh about the appellant 's confessing to him that he bad committed the murder of Sheo Swarup and not that of Sheo Shankar. The fact that the appellant did purchase a sword before the incident and deposited it with human blood at the Police Station on the night of the occurrence, is not sufficient to establish that it must be the appellant who committed the murders of Sheo by surprise. The mere possession of a sword so long as the mere possession was of a kind which leads to such a supposition does not necessarily lead to the inference that the person who possessed it immediately after the murder had enmity with Sheo Sahai, was holding that he did commit the murder. The extra judicial confession of the appellant to Ujagar Singh is corroborated by the evidence of Paley Singh, Palei Singh, and PaleY Singh, who deposed about the sale of a country made pistol at the police station. The High Court was wrong in rejecting his statement about the commission of the offence by the appellant. The evidence of the witnesses that the deceased Sheo Sahai had been murdered on account of enmity with the appellant is corroborated from the facts that the accused had a bath in the Canal at that hour. The circumstance that the blood stained weapon was found to be stained with human Blood immediately after murder and that the sword was handed over by the accused himself to the Police Officer at the Station, cannot be relied upon as it is not unlikely that the appel lant would have made a statement that he has committed the crime of murder.

The appellants filed a petition under Article 226 of the Constitution before the High Court challenging the validity of the electoral roll and the calendar events issued for the purpose of the election. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the entire election process had become vitiated on account of the defect in the notice issued under Rule 4(1) of the Rules notifying that claims and objections should be preferred within a period of 20 days from the date of publication of the notice under Rule 3(1). In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the declaration of results of all the 44 successful candidates was not in accordance with law, and (ii) the notification issued by the State Government under Rule 8 of the rules calling upon persons whose names had not been included in the electoral rolls and who claimed to be included in i.e., four candidates were illegal. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The declaration of result of all those successful candidates is liable to be quashed. [497B] 2. The notification issued under r. 4(i) of Rules by the Collector was published on November 25, 1978 and the poll was held on December 31, 1978. No satisfactory explanation was given in the course of the petition by the appellants as to why they delayed filing of the writ petitions till December 28, 1978 though they knew that there was an error in the notification under Rule (1) and that the delay in filing the petition should have been ignored. [498C D] 3. The expression "any other sufficient reason" occurring in r.4(3) of Madhya Pradesh Munici pal Corporation (Preparation, Revision and Publication of Electoral Rolls and Selection Rolls Rules, 1963 is not defined in the Act. It is a well settled rule of interpretation that unless there are words or expressions used in a statute which are capable of two interpretations, the Court should adopt the construction which would advance the object of the statute. [598D E] 4. The word "reason" has been used in the context of the Act to convey the idea of the legislature that it is not possible to lay down any precise definition of the expression. It must be interpreted in a broad and liberal spirit so as to advance the cause of justice. [500F G] 5. The object of section 4(3), which is intended to achieve, is to prevent the mischief of the provision by preventing improper acceptance or rejection of claims and to ensure that the election is not vitiated on any account of improper rejection or rejection. It does not contemplate a detailed enumeration of the grounds for the exercise of power under section 4. [699B C] 6. The purpose of section 5(3)(b) is to enable the voters to make their claims and/or objections thereto within a specified period. The provision in section 4, which is designed to achieve the object, must be construed in a manner which would promote the object sought to be achieved by the Act and not by way of an exception or a mere pretence. [511E] 7. The words "reason to believe" are used in section 5, which means "the reasonable belief". It is not necessary that the reasons should be communicated to the voters before they can be accepted as correct. The reason for the belief must be such as would advance public interest and good government. [504D E; 516A] 8. The requirement of section 6(3). is mandatory and it cannot be said that the grounds are not communicated to voters before the date on which the notification was issued. It has been held by this Court in several cases that the publication of a notice under r 4(l) of Rule 4 must be treated as sufficient compliance with the requirements of section 7(3); that the requirement of the section is mandatory; and that it cannot, therefore, be said to have been complied with. [525B C]. 9.

The appellants were directors of a company. The respondent company was incorporated in the year 1949 and its directors were also directors. In the year 1950, the respondent company filed a complaint against the appellants for failure to file a balance sheet and profit and loss account of the company as required under section 220(1) of the Companies Act 1913 or section 220 of the , which was punishable under sub section (3) of that section. The Magistrate acquitted the appellants on the ground that the prosecution under section 134 of the Act could not be launched against them because the general meeting had not been called and the balance sheet was not prepared. On appeal, the High Court held that since the general body meeting had been called before a general body there could be no question of that balance sheet being adopted nor complying with the requirements of section 220 and though wilful omission to call a general meeting and to lay the balance sheets and profit loss account before an annual general meeting was necessary. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The High Court was right in holding that the decision necessarily led to the conclusion that even in a prosecution under s 134 of 1913 Act the company and its Directors could not rely upon their failure as an answer to the charge and so, if he was responsible for not calling the general meetings before a meeting. [413 D] (2) The fact that section 26 makes the offence a continuing one and provides that after the balance Sheet is laid before a special general meeting it shall be open to the company at any general meeting to make an application to the Registrar of Companies for permission to file the balance Sheets and profit & loss account. [408 D] In the present case, the obligation to send a copy of the balance statement and profit or loss account was dependent on its being laid before the general general body. The High 'Court had taken a contrary view and followed the decision of this Court in Vulcan Industries (P) Ltd. vs Registrar of companies, Orissa, [1966] 1 S.C.R. 869. In that case the obligation was independent of the holding of a general meetings. But under section 131 of the 1913 Act, the liability to send the copy of balance sheet or profit and Loss account is dependent on the holding. The punishment under these sections is for default in filing copies of the Balance Sheet or profit & Loss account before the company in general meeting. If no balance sheet is laid after a general general meeting before which it is laid, a statement of fact and of that reason have to be annexed to the balancesheet and profitand loss account is entirely dependent on their being laid.

The respondents were tried by a Special judge for offences under section 302 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code and were convicted. The High Court confirmed their conviction but on appeal, it was contended that the provisions of the Act were discriminatory and violative of article 14 of the Constitution in so far as they purported to vest in the State Government an absolute and arbitrary power to refer to a special court for trial of certain offences or classes of cases; and that the classification based upon such a classification was not reasonable. Held, that the object of the impugned Act was to provide for speedier trial of offences and to make it more effective from the date of the commencement of the trial by a special judge and that it was intended to provide the speedi tory trial of those offences. The provisions of article 19(1)(g) of the Constitu tion were not intended to be exhaustive but only to cover cases where there was no special circumstances which could justify the classification. The object of section 5(1) of Act in so much as it empowered the State government to direct "cases" to be tried by Special Courts according to the special procedure provided by it for the spe cial trial of such offences, was not a good enough classification and therefore the provisions were not discriminatory. Held further, that there was nothing in article 14 which prevented the State from making any provision for the imposition of a special procedure for the trial of specified offences. It is well settled that the power to make rules under article 309 of the Consti tution is discretionary and must be exercised with caution and only when it is shown that the legislature has used its own language in order to give effect to the policy of the law. The State Government can only select those cases which, in their opinion, require a speedi er trial of an offence or class of offences or class o f them from another offence or classes or classes and cases may be tried on a special basis according to such procedure as it thinks fit. The classification based on such a class of cases must also be made in the light of the object for which the Act is enacted, namely, that it is intended to give speedi d trial of the offences; and in the opinion of the legislature certain offences may require more expeditious trial than those under trials.

The appellant was appointed as an Assistant Professor of Radiology in the Irwin Hospital, New Delhi. He was promoted to the post of Associate Professor of the concerned speciality on the recommendation of a Departmental Promotion Committee. The appellant was selected and appointed as Professor of Physiology (ex officio) in the said speciality. In the year 1973 he was promoted as an Associate Professor in the Department of Radiologist. On his promotion as Professor, he was again promoted to that post. He challenged the order of promotion before the High Court by a writ petition contending that the designation of the appellant as a Radiologist cum Associate Professor was akin to that of Honorary Professor or Associate Professor and that the appellant who had been substantively appointed to the said post of Professor of Pathology (exZaminating) in Maulana Azad Medical College, NewDelhi, was also entitled to be considered for appointment to the same post. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the post held by the appellant was a teaching post and that he was not eligible for appointment as Professor or Assistant Professor in any supertime grade of Radiologists. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the Union of India, that the nature of duties performed by the post graduate doctors were different and the appellant had been rightly appointed to that office. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The Ministry of Health cannot be heard to say that the appel lant possessed the requisite experience for appointment in supertime Grade II for a non teaching job. [8H; 8A] 2. The post of Radiological Officer cum Associate Professors in Maheed Azad Medical college is akin to the posts of Professor and Assistant Professor, and they are entitled to the benefit of the Second Schedule. [9B C] 3. The letter dated February 23, 1974 addressed by the Ministry of Home Affairs to the appellant clearly shows that the Ministry had been utilising his services as such for teaching the post Graduate and under graduate students of the Maulana Nehru Medical College for the M.D., M.S. D.M.S., New Delhi, for the academic year 1973 74. The said letter also shows that it was intended to be used by the Government of India in the Health Department of the Central Health Service as a teaching job for the last 17 years. [10E F] 4. It is not possible to accept the contention that the duties performed on the post are different and, therefore, the appellant cannot claim the status of an Associate professor cum Professor of radiology (Ex officio) by parity of reasoning. [11F G] 5. The Government of indi cially decided to treat the teaching experience gained by the appe lant as a research job for a period of 17 years and to extend the benefit thereof to him. [12G H; 13A B] 6. The Central Health Services (Amendment) Rules, 1966 are not intended to apply to the case of the Appellant who is a Radiographer cum Associate professor or Radiologist in Mahants ' College. [14E F]. 7. The provisions of the Indian Medical Council Act, 1956 which have been enacted by Parliament under Entry 66 of List I of Seventh Schedule of the Constitution do not give him any right to hold the post as Professor and/or Assistant Professor either in super time or in a non clinical hospital. [15F G; 15A] 8. The question whether a specialist grade II is eligible for promotion or appointment as a Professor or an Associate Dean of the speciality in the Maheed undergoing Medical College does not give the appellant a right to claim the post and the mere designation of that appellant as such does not gives him a right of hold the said posts as such. [16F G].

The workmen of the appellant company were employed by the management of a Cement Plant at Rajgangour in the State of Orissa. The Company was incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913 and its undertakings were taken over by the Government of India. The workmen of both these companies were paid wages at the rates fixed by the Tribunal. The dispute between the parties related to the fixation of minimum wage of the workmen of two 678 categories of workers. The Tribunal held that the minimum wage in the Company was Rs. 95 and not Rs. 96 as claimed by the workmen, but it took into account the fact that there were other industries in the same line of business as the Company in the region which could be compared with the Company. On appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The Tribunal committed no error of law requiring interference by this Court by basing its decision on the principle contained in the earlier Agreement of 1959. [677 E] (ii) The principle which is applied is the simple one of calculating the bonus payable at the rate of three months basic wages and dearness allowance. In the case of even the lowest paid clerical staff to whom dearness allowance is separately payable, the bonus is only calculated on the basis of basic wages, and the dearness allowance was ignored. [678 C] (iii) The fact that under the Agreement of 1960, the workmen and the Company had specifically agreed to exclude these classes of workers in regard to payment of bonus would not make any difference because, according to the workmen the calculation was still on the foundation of basic wage, because it cannot be assumed that their wage is a consolidated wage consisting of two 677 categories of basic pay and dearness allowances. [676 E] The Tribunal was expected to decide the dispute only as referred to it and at the time of reference, at least there could not possibly be a claim for higher bonus on the ground that under an Agreement of 1958, the workman and the company had specifically to exclude those classes of workmen in regard tO payment of Bonus. [674 G] (iv) The High Court was right in holding that there was no justification to introduce a new element of payment of wages to casual and badi workers at this stage.

The assessee was carrying on business as a partnership firm. The Income tax Officer issued a notice under section 148 of the Indian Income tax Act, 1961 to the assessee for initiating proceedings against him for the assessment year 19 19. The assessee filed an application before the Income tax officer for issuing a notice to show cause why he should not be assessed to income tax for the years 19 19 and 20. The Assistant Commissioner rejected the application holding that the notice was invalid as it did not comply with the requirements of section 148(2) of the Act. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the assessee had failed to produce the records of the Income Tax Officer before he issued a second show cause notice under s 148 and that the order sheet recording the reasons of the income tax officer was invalid inasmuch as it does not complywith the requirements Of section 148. The Tribunal dismissed the application. In appeal, by special leave, HELD : (i) The order sheet recorded the reasons for issuing the second show notice under S 148. [448 C] (ii) The material that he had before him for issuing notice under Section 148 is not mentioned in the report. He did not record himself that he was satisfied that this was a fit case for issue of a notice. [449 E F] (iii) The Tribunal has rightly held that it is a fit one for the issue of the notice under sec. 148. In his report the Income ' tax Officer does not set out any reason for coming to the conclusion on the material before him that this is a case for the issuance of a second notice under Sec. 148, but he merely noted the word "yes" and affixed his signatures thereunder.

The appellant, a partnership firm carrying on business in the State of Madras, was assessed to income tax for the years 1948 49 and 1949 50. The Income tax Officer treated the said firm as a separate entity under section 25(4) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the firm had been dissolved and its business was carried on thereafter by two independent firms, for the document of October 30, 1943, referred to annexures C 1 and C 11 as constituting two independent partnerships and proceeded to revoke them and provided that both the parties to the instrument "have (1) agreed to carry on and continue as one single partnerships, and (2) that the parties should have been given a further right to the assessee but with that right he was not liable to pay tax for any period between April 13, 1938 and March 28, 1939. The appellant 's appeal to the Appellate Assistant Com missioner was dismissed by the Income tax Appellate Tribunal. On reference the High Court held that as a result of this splitting up there was a discontinuance of the original business at the date of partition and on such discontinuance the family became entitled to relief under section25(4). In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The two sub sections give a further power to the Income Tax Officer to revoke or modify an earlier order if he is satisfied that there was no succession. [107 D] (ii) The words "as soon as may be" in section 25 of the Act are wide enough to include a change of ownership of all businesses and it is not necessary that there should be a succession only to the business which had paid tax under the Act of 1918. [108 E F] (iii) The word 'transfer ' in section 2(4)(a) means transfer of property in goods for cash or deferred payment or other valuable consideration. It does not include any transfer of an interest in goods. The word "transfer" is used in a wide sense to denote transfer of all kinds of property and it includes a transfer of one kind of property. [111 F] Commissioner of Income tax, Bombay City vs R.M.D. Chamarbaugwala, ; , referred to. (iv) The expression 'transfer of property ' in the section means transfer by way of sale or mortgage for cash, deferred payment, or other consideration. The words 'as soon may be ' are wide and they do not include a transfer by the assessee of any interest in the goods. [112 F G] Commissioner Of Income tax vs RM. Chamarotiwala, , referred lo.

The appellant 's father, who was the son of his predeceased son, executed a will in favour of his two sons. The properties were divided between him and his two brothers by metes and bounds. In the partition deed dated March 19, 1975, the widow 's share was given to her husband 's brother. The appellant filed a suit for partition and separate possession of the properties. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the suit properties belonged to the joint family and that there was no prior partition and that the plaintiff is entitled to a 7/24th share. On appeal, the High Court held that the decree passed by the trial court was not vitiated on account of any error apparent on the face of the record. In this appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that (i) in view of Explanation 1 to section 6 of the Hindu Succession Act, the interest of a Hindu Mitakshara coparcener shall be deemed to be the share in the property that would have been allotted to him if a partition of the property had taken place immediately before his death; and (ii) the High court was wrong in holding that on a true view of law, the wife 's shares must be ascertained by adding the share to which she is entitled at a notional partition during her husband life time and the share which she would get in her husbands ' life time. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The Explanation 1 does not contemplate that the interest in the coparcenary property should be deemed as the share of the deceased in the family property. [724 B] (2) In order to ascertain the share, of the appellant in the joint Hindu Family property on the hypothesis of a partition between himself and his sons, the two sons, there would be four sharers in the Joint Hindu Family Property. The first step is to find out the share when the deceased had in the coparcener 's family life time because after all, the plaintiff has a 1/4th share in that coparcenary property. In order that the heirs of the testator should get their or her share in it, the appellant ' s share therein will be 1/6th.

The appellant Corporation was incorporated under the Companies Act, 1956. The employees of the Corpo ration were transferred to the Corporation on or after 1st September, 1956 and they joined service in the Corporation as Class I and Class II. On 1st October, 1956, the Corporation issued a notification under section 49(2) of the Act appointing the employees of Class I & Class II as its employees. The appellant Corporation made an application to the Life Insurance Corporation for premature retirement on the ground that the employees were not entitled to continue in service beyond 60 years of age and that the said Authority had no power to extend the period of compulsory retirement. The Corporation rejected the claim of the employees and directed the Corporation to retire them on completion of 58 years of qualifying service. The Life Insurance Corpora tion challenged the order of the Corporation before the High Court which allowed the petition holding that the employee of Class II and Class III who had entered service of the Corpora tration after 1 st September, 1955 was not entitled for continue in serv ice beyond 60 days of age. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant Corporation that since he had the right to continue upto 60 years as a class III employee only till he attained the age of 60 years, the age ous retirement in his case could not be reduced to 58 years only because he had been promoted to Class I post after 1.9. 1956 and that therefore the age Of superannua tion should be raised to 60 years only. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: The High Court erred in striking down regulation 19(2), as amended in 1977, and directing the Corporation not to continue the service beyond the age 58 years merely because he has been promoted earlier to Class III post after January 1, 1956 by the Corporatio tion. [188B C] In the instant case, the appellant corporation was incorporated on 1st November, 1956 under the provisions of the Companies Ac tions Act, 1913 and the amendment of Regulation 19(1) by the new sub regulation was made in the year 1977. The amendment of the Regulations was made by the old sub regulation which came into force on September 3, 1966. [189C D] The amendment made by Regulation 19 (2) was not retrospective in operation so as to affect the existing employees who had joined service after 1th September,1956.

The appellants wrote a letter to the President of India with copies to the Prime Minister, Chief Justice of India and the Chief Justice. The appellants were informed that the matter would be placed before the Chief Minister for his comments. The Chief Justice was requested to send a copy of the letter to all the Judges of the High Court. The letter was signed by 15 members of the Bar Association of Charkhi Dadri. The appellant wrote a letters to the Chief Secretary, Government of Haryana and the Prime Ministers. The President informed them that the case would be listed before the Hon 'ble Chief Minister on the day fixed for hearing. The matter was placed before another Chief Minister who sent a letter dated 20th February 1975 to the then Prime Minister. The High Court did not take any action against the appellants on the letter written by five members of Bar Association, Bhiwani. The letters were signed by the President and the other Ministers. In the meanwhile, the Chief Ministers wrote to the Governor that the cases would be put up before the next sitting Judge for hearing on the question whether the case should be listed in the next session or not. The Governor sent a copy to all Judges of this Court. On receipt of the letters, the High COurt directed the Chief Secretaries to send copies of the same to the Union Government. The Union Government filed appeals against the order of the Full Bench. The Division Bench dismissed the appeal and held that the letter was not a contempt of court. In these appeals by special leave it was contended for the appellants that the contents of the Letters were unchallenged, that the letters did not constitute contempt of Court; that the High Courts had no jurisdiction to punish the appellants because they were guilty of contempt of the Court; and that the appellants had failed to prove their case beyond reasonable doubt. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: (1) The letter of the appellant and the said Ministers addressed to them by the deponent to the president of India cannot be construed as scandalising the Honble Judge or the Chief Justices in any manner to weaken people 's faith in the administration of justice. [243F] (2) The letters did constitute contempt. The contents thereof a prima facie case contempt is made out. The apology tendered by the appellants was accepted by the High court. The deponent had tendered his apology to this Hon ' ble Court for the same and prayed for its acceptance.

The petitioner, Suraj Mall Mohta and Co. (P) Ltd., was assessed to income tax for the assessment years 1947 48, 1948 49 and 1949 50 under section 5(1) of the Income tax Act, 1922. The petitioner contended that the provisions of the Taxation on Income (Investigation Commission) Act, 1947, were void as they contravened article 14 Of the Constitution inasmuch as in the case of persons coming within the ambit of sub section (4) of section 5 as persons to a substantial extent evaded payment of taxation on income, or (b) that some other points other than those referred to under section 6(1), by the Central Government or the Commission were not referred to it by the Commission. Held: (i) The provisions of section 34 of the Indian Income tax and Excess Profits Tax Act, 1940, are not ultra vires article 14 of the Constitution as they are inconsistent with the provisions Of article 20(3) of that Article. The provisions in sub section 4 of section 6 of the impugned Act are not violative of article 14 because they are not severable from those of other provisions of law and do not offend against article 14. (ii) The words "any person" in sub s.(4) Of section 5 of the Act are wide enough to include persons who have evaded payment or evaded payment. The expression "any other person" is used in the context of the present case as including those who have escaped assessment and whose cases were referred to by the commission under section 34(1). The provisions contained in sub sections (4), (7) and (8) of s 5 are not intended to be exhaustive but only cover persons who may evaded payment, or evaded evasion of tax. The words used in sub cls. (a) to (e) of cl. (3) are wide and they do not include persons whose cases are referred to in section 5. The word "person" is defined in the Act as including a company or association or body of individuals. It includes a firm, a firm or a Hindu undivided family. The definition of "company" in section 2(h) of 'the Indian Income Tax Act includes a company and every person who has evaded payment by reason of fraud or collusion or any other similar act is liable to pay income tax on the basis of his total income. The Income tax Officer, while assessing the petitioner under section 4(1)(a), was not required to give reasons for making an assessment. He had no power to add to the number of persons included in section 6 (1) by the impugned notification. The proviso to sub section 2 of section 4 which provides that subject to the provisions contained therein, the Commission shall have power to amend the number specified in the report submitted under section 7 and to make such alterations as it thinks fit. The effect of this provision is that the Commission may add to or delete from the total income any person included in the assessment for any year. It is not necessary that the proviso should be read as a whole so as to include all persons who are liable to tax under section 3(1); but the proviso does not say that it shall be applicable only to those cases where the total number of partners exceeds ten, but does not exceed ten. The petitioners were carrying on business in the name and style of Suraj Mall Mota Co., Ltd., which was a registered firm. They had evaded payment for the years 1947 49 and 1948 50 under the provisions section 5 (1). They had been assessed to tax for that year by the Income Tax Officer, but they did not pay any heed to their request.

The appellant, a non commercial establishment, carried on the business of manufacturing and selling textiles. The Federation was registered under the Delhi Shops and Establishments Act, 1954. The appellant was a "commercial establishment" within the meaning of section 2(5) of the Act. In the course of its business, the appellant was engaged in the manufacture and sale of textiles. It was also doing so by way of selling textiles and cloth. The Chief Inspector of Shops and Establishment, Delhi, called upon the Federation to register its establishment 'he under the Act, but the Federation failed to comply with the direction and filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the order of the Chief Inspector. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the activities carried on by the Federation were not "a business or trade" within section 2 (5) Of the Act and that the appellant 's activities amounted to "work in connection with, or incidental or ancillary to trade" under the definition of "commercial Establishment". In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the activity of the Federation carried on in these premises was a business or profession within the definition section 2 of the . HELD: (i) The High court was right in holding that it was not an "establishment" as defined in section 2. (5). [353 E] (ii) The activities of the Union are also in the nature of material services within the wider definition of 'commercial establishment ' given in the Act.[353 G] (iii) The concept of "industrial establishment" is a well known and accepted connotation from the decisions of this Court. In order to constitute an industry it must be shown that it has been engaged in any activity which is not merely incidental or incidental to trade, but also some activities which are incidental or connected with or ancillary thereto. [353 G H] (iv) The definition of the word "trade" in section2(5), includes the idea of profit, yet the definition is of a mere word 'business ' and it would bear repetition that the Federation also publishes periodicals, bulletins etc. and issues the same to members free of this court free of the present case as set out in its Memorandum of Association.

The assessee was a Hindu undivided family headed by one Sri Trivikram Narain Singh who was the original founder and owner of what is known as Ausanganj State in the district of Benaras. The income tax Officer held that it was a regular income of the assessee and did not fall within the category of agricultural income tax. He, however, held that the receipt of the income from land, rent or collections from land was not agricultural income for "although the pension was determined with respect to the quantum of the rent collection the rent or the land could not be said to be the immediate source of the pension. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner and the Tribunal confirmed the order of the Income tax Officer. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The source of income is clearly the arrangement arrived at in 1837 and therefore it is not agricultural Income as defined in the Act. [703 B] (ii) The income of a fraction of the net income of an estate or land revenue is liable to tax under the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. It follows from the decisions of this Court that if it is held in this case that the source of such allowance or pension is the arrangement entered into in 1838 and therefore, it is difficult to hold that the receipts of the assesee were agricultural income within the meaning of section 4(3)(viii) of the Act, the source being the amount of income still the arrangement remains the arrangement and not land. [074 C D] (iii) The expenditure of the allowance varied from year to year, the nature of the property appropriated as remuneration is not in the right to receive rent or revenue of agricultural lands but rests in the covenant in the deed to receive remuneration for management of the trust.

The petitioners in the writ petitions were appointed as Chargemen 'A ' in various departments of the State Government. They were promoted to officiate as Chargeman II and some of them have even been promoted to higher posts. The petitioners in their writ petitions flied a writ petition before this Court praying for a direction to the respondents to give them promotion from the date they completed two years ' service as Supervisor A '. This Court by its order dated 2nd February, 1981 allowed the writ peti tion and directed that the petitioners would be entitled to all consequential benefits including seniority and promotion. The High Court also directed that in future promotions of all such Supervisors who had been recruited in 1963 and those who had already been promoted as Charge Man ov er, should not be disturbed. In the appeals by special leave it was contended for the peti tioners that since Rule 8 of the Rules contemplated a Supervisor 'A to have been appointed as Supervisor 'B ' on completion of two years service as Supervisors 'A, they were entitled to be considered for promoti tional promotion only on completion o f two years of continuous service. Dismissing the writ petition, this Court, HELD: 1. The seniority list prepared in accordance with the rules was not challenged by any of the petitioners. [109F] 2. Rule 8 is a self contained code and it has to be read as a whole. It is settled law that there has to he nat urely a Supervisor who claims promotion as Charge II and others have even foughed in service. The rule does not require that the Supervisor 'C ' should have been promoted on completion Of two years s of continuous serv ice as Supervisor. [110B] 3. Rule 10 of the Madhya Pradesh Hi gh Court Rules, 1966 is a well settled rule of interpretation and it cannot be said that there is no room for any intendment in the matter of promotion. It has to b een held that the rules are not intended to be retrospective merely because they have been framed by the State Govern ment in consultation with the Public Service Commission. [111G H] 4. The principle of interpretation is well settled and it is not open to a Court to ignore the language employed by the legislature. It may also be noticed that even though the petition ers on their completion of 2 years ' serv ice were not promoted as Supervisor, they had been given a proper place in the gradation list havi ng deemed to be promoted to the higher post with effect from the dates they completed the two yea rs of service. [112H; 113A B] 5. The respondents have not been able to make out any case for interference by this Court in the exercise of its jurisdiction under Article 136 of the Constitution.

The Karnataka State Road Transport Corporation (Acquisition of Motor Vehicles) Act, 1976 was enacted to provide for the acquisition and disposal of motor vehicles in the State of Karnataka. Section 47(1 H) provides that where in pursuance of an approved scheme, a State Transport Undertaking applies for a stage carriage permit from a State transport undertaking for operating in any inter State route, the authority is satisfied that the State Transport Authority would be able to operate in the inter State routes without detriment to its responsibility to provide efficient and adequate road transport services in any notified area or notified route. Section 48(1) provides for preference to applications for permits from other States. The appellant Corporation was constituted under the Act, which was a nationalised State Road Traffic Board. The State Transport Appellate Tribunal set aside the orders of the State Government and directed the State Road Services Authority to hear the appeals and dispose them of in accordance with law after considering the claims of the applicants in the manner indicated in Sher Singh 's case and now. In the appeals by special leave, it was contended for the appellant Corporation that the High Court and the State Appellate Tribunal were wrong in distinguishing the decision of this Court in Sher singh vs Union of India, ; that the general scheme of the Act in the matter of grant of permits for stage carriages and contract carriages appears to be that except in the case of a notified route or notified area where under section 68 F(1), the permit has to necessarily be granted to the State transport Undertaking. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The general scheme is that the application for stage carriage permits from the State to the private operators should have preference in the matters of stage carriage. [1015B] 2. The special scheme of section 47(i H) does not say for example, for like section 68F(1). The general rule of preference and says that an application for permit from the Indian Tourism Development Corporation, the State Tourist Department were not questioned but the preference provided for by clause (iv) of the proviso to section 63(7), is unconstitutional and so it is declared unconstitutional. [1051C] 3. The scheme of Section 47 (1 H), which prescribes that in pursuance to an approved Scheme, a Regional Transport Authority in any other case, will have preference, while under the latter the State or the State tourist Department would have preference. [ 1015D E] 4. The exclusion contemplated by section 68 H(1H) applies with equal force to the preference available for applications from the other States and the Regional Transport Authorities in any of the other cases. [1006B C] 5. The reservation contemplated by Section 47 H is confined to persons who have applied for stage Carriage permits. The preference is confined only to persons whose claims are approximately equal. [1105D] 6. The proviso to Section 63(1 A) applies equally with equal effect to the priority provided in section 47 (i H). The exclusion envisaged by Section 68F (1H), therefore, applies with full regard to all eligible applicants and not with reference to the preferential preference provided in Section 47H. [1151E] 7. The provision for preference is limited to persons other than those who have already applied for Stage Carriage permits under section 48(i) of Act. [1025D F] 8. The word 'preference ' occurring in Section 48 (1) H, in the back ground of the provisions of Chapters IV and IV A, does not mean that the preference should be confined to operators of tourist cars and travel agents. [1035E] 9. The expression 'preference ' occurring therein is wide enough to include all persons who are eligible for stage Carriages and travel agent. [995F G] 10. The object of Section 48 is to enable the State Governments to provide transport services to the public at large, and to make provision for the better and efficient road transport service in any area or route.

The respondent was a dealer in the business of selling and distributing goods. The registered instrument provided that the tax payable by him shall be paid in such manner and in such instalments, if any, as may be specified in the notice of assessment not being less than fifteen days from the date of service of the notice. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the Act on the ground that it was ultra vires the power of the State Government under sections 19(1) and (2) of the Madras General Sales Tax Act, 1939. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that Rule 21 A was ultra rites. In appeal to this Court, HELD : Rule 21A is beyond the rule making power of a State Government either under section 19(i) or section 19 (2)(c) of tho Act. [665 B] The word 'assessment ' used in section 19 of the is charging section. It follows that the State has authority under its rule making powers under section19(1), and (b) of tile Madras General sales Tax Act 1939 to create a legal fiction by which the transferee of the business is constituted as the dealer liable to pay the tax. [663 C] The words 'assessment " in section 20(2)(a) are wide enough to include assessment, reassessment or collection of tax from any other person other than a dealer. It is manifest that a person who purchases a business as a dealer can be assessed to sales tax only in respect of his turnover and under the scheme of charging provision of the enactment of the purchaser of the goods liable to tax.
