The word "assessment" used in the section means assessment, re assessment or collection. [664 D] The State Government had power under section 20 (1) to frame the impugned rule. It was not intended that the legislature would have intended that it should be prospective and retrospective. The words "assessment " occurring in section 10(2) were wide enough. They could not be used to enlarge the scope of section 10 regarding recovery and payment of tax. There is no reason why the Legislature should not have intended to confer a legal right on the transferee to recover the arrears of sales tax due by him from the transferor. [661 D E] The expression "assessment ' in section 2(a) means assessment or re collection of taxes. It does not include reassessment or recovery of tax and it is open to the State to make rules to carry out the purposes of the statute but the section cannot be utilised to enlarge scope of that section regarding recovery.

The appellant was a public servant. He was dismissed from service by an order dated February 2, 1955, passed by the Inspector General of Prisons, Saurashtra, under section 3(1) (a) of the Bombay Reorganisation Act, 1960. The appellant filed a suit for a declaration that he was in Government service till the date of the suit only and there will be a decree for Rs. 1,000/ . The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court on appeal reversed it holding that the failure to supply a copy of the report of the Enquiry Officer amounted to denial of reasonable opportunity contemplated by article 311(2) of 'the Constitution. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The order of dismissal was truly a liability in proceedings relating to a contract within section 60(2)(a) and it was not necessary for the appellant to show that he had actually been in Government Service till the appointed day. [922 D] (ii)The High Court erred in holding that there had been a breach of article 311 (2) Of the Constitution. The order passed by it was based on contract within the meaning of section 60 of the Act and not under section 61. [936 C] (iii)The appellant 's liability to pay arrears of salary is not a liability arising out of a contract but was a liability for that State. [946 D E] (iv) The High Court was wrong in holding, on the facts, that there was no duty to supply the copy of a report of Enquiry Officer. [948 G H] (v)The order passed in the present case did not amount to denial or violation of reasonable opportunities contemplated by Article 311(1).

The appellant was the owner of a coal mine and had been using it for mining purposes. The respondents were lessees in respect of coal mines situated within the area of the appellant. The appellant claimed that the respondents had encroached upon their coal mines on the northern side and removed coal from the boundary line between them. The trial court held that the appellant was entitled to a decree for possession of the land and mesne profits. On appeal, the High Court reversed the finding of fact arrived at by the courts below and decreed the suit. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appel lant that the High Courts had erred in holding that the burden of proof was on the respondents beyond the prescribed time and that the onus was on them to prove that they had knowledge of the encroachment only within three years thereof. Held, that the finding arrived at on the assumption that the initial burden of proving that the respondent came to know of the removal of coal by the appellant or their possession of coal removed beyond three years prior to the suit was wholly erroneous and must be set aside. The High Court had rightly held that there was no evidence on record to show that the encroachment was prior to 1932, but there was also no acceptable evidence on the part of the respondents to establish that they came to knowledge of removal of the coal by them or their occupation of the encroached area. Held further, that in view of the finding on the question of onus of proof, the burden was on both sides and the High court had rightly found that the appellants had failed to discharge the initial onus of proving the fact that the land was left in the encroached areas. The mere fact that a plot of land is not appurtenant to the land cannot be held to be conclusive evidence of the fact as to whether it has been encroached upon by the respondent or his predecessors in interest.

The appellant was employed as a crosscutter in Kozihkode in 824 the State of Kerala. He was caught hold by other workmen and taken outside. The Secretary and others threatened them with physical violence. The appellant terminated the services of the Secretary and another workman on July 8, 1958. The Industrial Tribunal held that the appellant had intended to take disciplinary action against the workman but subsequently departmental proceedings were dropped and action was taken under r. 18(a) of the Standing Orders. The Tribunal also held that there was no attempt at holding any departmental inquiry and therefore its action could not be upheld as a bona fide exercise of the power conferred by r. 17 (a). Held, that the Industrial Court had jurisdiction to intervene and set aside such termination. The employer could defend the action under r 18(b) on the ground that in a case of this kind the requirement of bona fides was essential and if the terminaton of service was a colourable exercise of power or the power was a device to get rid of an employee instead of following the course of holding an inquiry for misconduct, notice for which had been given to the employee and for which a departmental enquiry was intended to be held and decided to discharge the employee under r, 18 (a) it was not colourable exercise. The decision of this Court in the case of M/s. Bharat Bank Ltd., vs Their Workmen, ; , relied on. Held further, that in view of the decisions of this court in the cases referred to above, the employer could not defend the proceedings under r: 18(c) on grounds other than those mentioned in r. 19 (a), and if it was satisfied that the action taken under such a rule was colourable exercise, the industrial tribunal would have jurisdiction to interfere and set it aside such dismissal.

The appellants, who were the owners of a cinema theatre in Ahmedabad, filed a suit for declaration that they were entitled to a decree for possession of the cinema theatre and for an injunction restraining the defendants from enforcing their rights under the agreement dated December 1, 1960. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court held that the consent decree was not binding on the parties as it did not decide whether the agreement between them was in the nature of a lease or other character. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The question whether the legal relationship arising out of the agreement was in fact a lease could be decided only by consent decree of December 1. 1960. [457 D] (ii) The agreement dated November 27, 1954 created a lease and that the agreement did not determine the rights of the parties with reference to the agreement of December I, 1960, but it was for the Trial Court in the first instance to decide that question and allow the whole question to go into that question or to decide whether there after the High court could, if the matter were brought before it by way of appeal or in exercise of its revisional jurisdiction, have decided that question. [441 E] (iii) The consent decree operated as res judicata because it was not a judgment by consent order of December l, 1960 and it was only for the trial Court to decide the question over again to the extent to which the court, viz., the trial court in the earlier suit, proposed to go behind that decision.

The respondent was appointed as a Pilot Officer in the Indian Air Force on 1.6.1972 and was confirmed in that post on 30.8.1985. He was later promoted to the post of Assistant Controller of Defence Accounts on 26.7.1988. The respondent challenged his reversion before the High Court contending that he was entitled to be reinstated in service on the pronouncement of the Judgment on 24.3.1988 notwithstanding the fact that his term of office had come to an end on 30th August, 1985 and not beyond that date unless there was a further extension. The High Court allowed the Review Peti tion Petition holding that the order could not be sustained and the Writ Petition was liable to be allowed. Aggrieved by the said decision of the High court, the respondent filed a Special Leave Petition before this Court contending inter alia that he had been granted permanent commission in the Air Force and was working as a pilot Officer. The State of Uttar Pradesh also adopted the same scheme for the benefit of ex military officials. Dismissing the Special Leave petition, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High court while setting aside the order dated 26.8 .1988 directed that the respondent be entitled to salary upto the period he was appointed in Government service. [243F] 1.2 In the instant case, the interim order did not and could not amount to a direction that the respond ent was entitled only to remain in service. The interim order does not and cannot amount to an order on Review on 26th July, 1988. It is open for the opposite parties to consider the claim of the respondent for a continution in service or the fresh appointment and no observations in this regard are being made by this Court. [244A B] 1:3 The High Courts while setting at naught the interim orders dated 10.7 1986 passed in the Writ Peti tions filed by the respond er, had not urged before the Court that the said interim order could and did not amount lo a direction to that effect. It was open for him to consider his claim of reinstatement in service irrespective of the merits of the case and the extent of his right.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 Indian Penal Code and sentenced to suffer imprisonment for life. The High Court acquitted him on the ground that there were conflicting versions given by the prosecution and the defence and when two views were possible, the benefit of doubt should be given to the accused. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the discrepancies in the evidence of P. W. 1 and 3 which were corroborated by the evidence in the case of the prosecution had been sufficiently magnified by the Sessions Judge; (2) the discrepancy noticed by the High Court was of a minor character and that they have been unduly magnified; (3) the High court should not interfere with the order of acquittal merely because another view is also possible. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The discrepancies in evidence of the witnesses on the basis of which the Trial Court rejected the prosecution evidence are reasonable. [368C] 2. The Sessions Judge was well justified in commenting that the discrepancies on the foundation of the conviction of the accused must have been upset by persistent refusal of the brother and mother of the deceased to send her with him to his house. [369E F] 3. The evidence of PW 1, 2 and 3 who were the neighbours of the locality, was more probable than the version of the occurrence. They had also given a beating to the appellant to send him with her to his home. It is obvious that he must have had been upset at the persistent refusal by the brother or mother of P W. I to send the deceased with him. The injury must have caused in the manner suggested by the defence. [370F G] 4. The injuries on the person of the victim could not have been caused in any manner suggested either by the appellant or by the witnesses. It was, therefore, essential that any view of the evidence should be reasonable. If the evidence is so strong against the accused, the High Courts should not interference with the orders of acquittal simply because another views are possible. [371F G; 371A] 5. The appeal must accordingly fail.

The appellant, a public servant, was convicted by the Special Judge for an offence under section 5(1)(e) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The High Court acquitted him on the ground that he had failed to prove his innocence and that he was not entitled to any protection under Article 14 of the Constitution. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that: (i) Section 6(1) (c) of Prevention of corruption Act,1947 is not applicable to the case of a Judge of the Supreme Court or of the High Court under which a Judge can be removed from his office by an order of the President passed after an address by each House of Parliament supported by a majority of not less then two thirds of the members of that House and by a minority of not more then two fourths of members of the House present and voting has been presented to the President in the same session for such removal on the grounds of proved misbehaviour or incapacity; (ii) Section 7(1A)(c) is inappliable to a Judge who, if one may so describe it, is to be found only in article 2 read with Article 124(4) and (5) of tho Constitution. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The word 'may ' used in clause (e) has to be construed as meaning 'shall '. It must not be interpreted in a narrow or pedantic sense. [216B] 2.1 In order that the Parliament may use the word 'shall" it is necessary to consider the feasibility of the grant of sanction under section 6(i)(c). The words 'may be so construed ' are strong enough to take within their sweep every kind of cases which can be said to have been dealt with by the Legislature. [217D] 2:2. In order to find out whether a particular provision is mandatory or directory, the legislature must consider the question as to what would be the disproportion and his inability to account satisfactorily. The words in clause(e) have to be given some meaning which would place the burden on the prosecution, howsoever light, to make out a prima facie case for obtaining sanction of the competent authority under section6 of the Act and this can be done only if it is read as a part of the scheme under which the public servant is required to furnish particulars of his assets with reference to which the disproportion is required. [218E F] 2(a) The word "may" in clause 4 of Article 124 has to receive a liberal construction so as to advance the object and purpose of the statute. It cannot be interpreted to mean that the legislature may use its language in order to advance its object. [220D E] (b) In the instant case, the framers of the constitution while dealing with such constitutional functionaries did not fall within the purview of the expression 'may" as contemplated by clause 4(e). The word may be construed in a broad and liberal sense. It is for this reason that the framers have used the word "shall". [220E F; 221A] (c)(i) In order there should be some meaning to be assigned to it. The expression 'shall not be construed literally or narrowly, but must be understood in its popular sense. The context in which the word is used may indicate that the Legislature has used the words in a particular sense. If the language of the provision is plain and unambiguous, the court should look at the whole scheme under the Act to find what it intends to achieve.

The appellant was a member of the Scheduled Castes. The respondent filed an election petition challenging the election on the ground that he belonged to a smaller group of Sunri caste and was excluded from the Schedule Caste specified in item 40. The Tribunal held that the appellant bore surname Saha but was excluded by reason of his being a Sunri, and therefore, did not belong to the Scheduled Caste specified under item 40 and dismissed the election petition. On appeal, the High Court set aside the decision of the Tribunal and directed the election of the appellant to be set aside on the grounds that the respondent bore surnam Sahas within the fold of Sunrri caste. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appel lant: (1) The respondent had not been able to establish that he belongs to the category specified in Item 40 and therefore fell within the category of Scheduled Caste; (2) The Tribunal erred in holding that the Sahas were originally a smaller caste within the Sunri community, and (3) The evidence did not show that the said Sahas formed a sub caste strictly so called within the meaning of item 40, and, therefore, belonged to the appellant. HELD: (i) The correct interpretation of item 41 is that Sahas are really a distinct class of independent castes of Sunris. If the correct interpretation was accepted by the Tribunal it would be difficult to hold that the Legislature intended to exclude Sahas from the category mentioned in item 39. [391 D] (ii) The word 'include ' in the expression 'excluding Saha ' in item must, without more, refer to a caste group within the meanri caste but bore the surname. If a caste is a caste, the word ' spectrum ' in that item must be read as including those who belonged to that caste but bear the sur name. [392 E] (iii) The words 'excluding the Saha ' occurring in item 41 are not intended to cover Sahas also. It is only when the word "include" is used that it would mean a person belonging to a particular caste or tribe which has been included in the Schedule. If there is no such thing, then the word included must be given its ordinary meaning and must be construed as including something which is not included in it. [394 H] (iv) The expression 'including Saha ' used in item 42 means a person who belonged exclusively to a specified caste or community which has not been included therein. If therefore, the appellant was undoubtedly a member belonging to the said category he did not fall within the said class.

The appellant was a tenant of the respondent. The respondent filed a suit for eviction against the appel lant on the ground that he had agreed to pay rent to the appellant and that the appellant had agreed not to accept the rent. The trial court dismissed the suit but the High Court in appeal affirmed it. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The word "relinquishment" was used in the Transfer of Property Act and was used not in any strict technical sense but in its comprehensive meaning as giving up possession of the premises; and he pointed out that if it was intended by the legislature that "relul tial use should have the limited meaning sought to be placed upon it on behalf of the appellant, the word "surrender" used in section 108, sub clause (i), of the Trans fer Property Act would have been more appropriate. [422 D E] (ii) The definition of "relivish ment" in section 2(g) of the Transfer Of Property Act is wide enough to include a transfer by a tenant or any person acting on behalf o f the landlord to the transfer of a lease by sub lease or otherwise, and it provides that the landlord who receives any fine, premium or other like sum or deposit or any consideration for the grant, renewal or continuance of a tenancy would be guilty of an offence and liable to the punishment specified therein. [416 D E]. (iii) The term "relateinquishment", in section 18(1), is used in two parts: (a) it shall not be lawful for the tenant or person acting or purporting to act on behalf, of the tenant to claim or receive any sum or consideration as a condition of the relin quishment of his tenancy; and (b) it includes an assignment by the lessee of his rights as such.

The workmen of the appellant company were employed by the Union as clerks in the clerical cadre of the company. The workmen of both the companies were paid a consolidated wage scale of Rs. 150/ and Rs. 100/ respectively. The revised wage scales were revised to Rs. 125/ and the employees of the clerical staff in the category of Draftsmen and Rs 150/ in the case of other categories were given the benefit of the revised pay scales. The Industrial Tribunal, however, held that the existing wage scale was fair and reasonable and on a region cum industry basis and that it would not be possible for the appellant to bear the additional financial burden if the demands of the Union were accepted. On appeal by special leave, the appellant contended: (1) that the increase in paragraph 23 of the award was intended to apply only to each individual workman; (2) that while raising industrial disputes for revision of wage scales, it would obviously result in serious anomalous situations; and (3) that even if the demand of the union were accepted, the Tribunal had no power to revise the scales of pay and dearness allowance. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The Tribunal was betrayed by a curious confusion in accepting the plea of the respondent Union that a flat increase to the pay of each workman was intended in the original wage and consequently it fell into error of amending the award. [306 D] 2. The award of the Industrial Tribunal is clearly intended by the Tribunal as is evident from the reference to "flat increase of Rs 150" and "Rs. 100" in the instant case, a result wholly unwarranted, a consequence which would obviously be more concerned with the immediate benefits according to them. [307 E] 3. The increase in para 23 was intended only to apply to each workman; it could not be said that all the employees were to get additional pay of Rs 50/ or Rs 100/ in case of the category in the other categories. It cannot, therefore, be the case that the figure of Rs 15/ and of Rs 100 was intended by tho Tribunal as a flat enhancement of salary to all employees. [308 G H] 4. The fact that the workmen were paid Rs. 50/ and above the existing pay scale would not make any difference in the matter of wages. It is only when the wage scales are revised that the increased amount becomes more than what was actually paid by the workmen. [309 B C] 5. The additional financial liability if any, which may be incurred by the employer for the purpose of paying wages to all its employees would necessarily depend upon the nature and extent of the increase. It could not, therefore. be said to have been incurred in excess of what was originally paid. [310 D E] 6. The increased wage scale had necessarily to commence with figures Rs 150 and Rs 100 or in the cases of draftsmen and other workmen respectively, the revised wage scale having necessarily to start with figures RS. 150 and 100/. [300 F G] 7.

The appellant company was incorporated in the United Provinces of Bihar. The management of the company had entered into an agreement with the respondents, whereby it agreed to pay wages at the rate of Rs. 10/ per day and that the appellant paid its employees only. The terms of the contract provided that the workmen would be entitled to overtime wages at a certain percentage of their wages for every month. The appellant company claimed that the refusal of the appellant to pay them wages at rates higher than those prescribed by the award was illegal, because the rates of wages fixed by the said award did not fall within the definition of wages prescribed by section 2(vi) of the Act and that it had no jurisdiction to make any payment under the award. The respondents contended that the provisions of the Industrial Disputes Act were applicable to the case as they were governed by the terms of their contract, and that in view of the provisions contained in sections 23 and 29 of the , the appellant was not entitled to claim overtime wages for the period during which the company was closed down. Held: (i) The term "wages" is defined in section 2 (vi) as meaning all remuneration capable of being expressed in terms of money, which would if the terms Of money, were embodied in the contract of employment, express or implied. The word "wages ' has been used in a wide sense and it includes wages fixed under an award. It is not necessary that the term must be given its ordinary meaning and its ordinary connotation should be extended to all kinds of things which are capable of working as such. (ii)The definition of "wages " in section 3(vi), as it stood at the relevant time, provides that any remuneration payable under any award or settlement between the parties when they deal with disputes arising between them in respect of the said terms, Industrial adjudication is not bound to uphold the terms thereof, because, in substance, is the effect of industrial adjudication. The term 'wages ' is defined by section 3 (vi), and it means all remuneration which are incapable of being performed or which are not capable of performing any duty imposed on the employer by the Act. In a sense, the latter wage structure must be deemed to be a contract between the employer and the employees. If it is shown to the satisfaction of Industrial Tribunal that the terms prescribed by an award in law, and in substance constitute a fresh contract between parties when it deal with matters arising between the employers and their employees, there can be no doubt that the latter wages structure must he deemed to have been a contract of service, express and implied. (iii)The words "any remuneration" in section 15(vi)(a) are wide enough to include wages fixed for an employee under an agreement or settlement. The definition of 'wages" in the Act is not exhaustive but it includes all remuneration payable to an employee on account of his employment, such as wages, wages, etc., and it is not possible to lay down any general rule that wages should be paid by industrial adjudication only when they are related to a dispute between employers and employees. The expression "wages payable" in this definition has been defined in the Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 1946, as meaning wages which are payable to a workman under an employer.

The appellant was a Sub Divisional Officer in the Public Works Department, Pepsu. He was prosecuted under section 409 of the Indian Penal Code for having committed an offence punishable under section 465 and section 409 Of the Indian penal Code. The trial Magistrate acquitted him but on appeal the High Court convicted him under section 466 and section 467 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. On appeal by special leave to this Court, Held: (i) The sanction required under section 197(1) of the Criminal Procedure Code was necessary for prosecuting the appellant under section409 of the Penal Code. It is not necessary that the acts with which the appellant is charged directly bear on the duties which he has got to discharge as a public servant. The sanction is required under that section and it is only when the act complained of is directly concerned with his official duties so that, if questioned, it could be claimed to have been done by virtue of office. (ii)The appellant had not discharged any duty which he was bound to do in respect of the work entrusted to him. The fact that the appellant was discharging some duties which the respondent was required to discharge would not make him a public servants within the meaning of section 197 of the Cr. P.C. and the absence of such sanction is fatal to the maintainability of the prosecution. (iii)The sanction under section 196(1), Code of criminal Procedure, could be necessary for the prosecuting the accused under section 406 of the I.P.C., even though it might not have been necessary in all cases in which the official character of the person giving him an opportunity for the commission of the crime and those who had held it necessary when the offence was committed while the accused was actually engaged in the performance of his official duty. The appellant could claim to have paid the amount to Parma, and the acquittance roll records the payment, and there is in acknowledgment thereof a thumb impression as against his name. If what appears on the face of the roll is true and whether it is true or not is not a matter relevant at the stage of sanction, which mu_t precede the institution of the proceedings then the actswith which the accused is charged fall within the scope of his duties, and can be justified by him as done by him. (iv)The High Court was wrong in holding that the prosecution which had resulted in the conviction of the appellant could not be prosecuted under s.409 of Indian Penal code.

The appellant was a resident in Travancore State of Cochin. He was assessed to income tax for the assessment years 1949 50 and 1950 51 on the ground that he had incurred losses in the erstwhile State of Travancore Cochin. The Income tax Officer included the said loss as business profits under section 10(2)(c) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, but the Appellate Assistant Commissioner allowed the claim holding that the loss was not an 'Indian ' and that it was a revenue loss. On appeal by the appellant the Appellate Tribunal held that the losses incurred in the former State of Madras could not be set off against profits made in British India or other Indian States as the case may be, but that was done under section 8 of the Income tax (Amendment) Act, 1941 (XXIII of 1941). The High Court on reference held that business losses incurred by the assessee in the latter State of Kerala could not by virtue of proviso to section 24(1) of Travancore Act be set Off against profits and gains arising in British Indian States. Held, that the mere use of the words " income or gains accruing or arising to him within British India" in proviso (i) to section 14(2) of Income tax , 1922, meant business in British England and not business in Indian States and the profits and losses arising under the head business were taxable in India. The expression "income" in the proviso to sub section (1) Of section 14 of the Act means income accruing or arise within British Indian India and not in British British India. Commissioner of Income Tax, Bombay vs R. N. Balsara, , referred to.

The respondent company was incorporated in the Indian Companies Act, 1913. The Company was incorporated under the provisions of the Companies Act and its employees were governed by the provisions contained in section 3(1) (d) of the Act. Under section 3 of the , the age of retirement for workmen in all industries should be fixed at 60. In respect of the respondent company 's claim for fixing the age Of retirement at 60, the Company contended that it was agreeable to introduce for its Bombay employees similar provisions like those which had been introduced by agreement for the Calcutta Employees ' Union at the age 55 and that the trend had been to fix the age at 60 years. The Tribunal rejected this contention and held that the company was entitled to fix its age of superannuation at 60 and that it could not be said that the practice of fixing the retirement age at 58 was incorrect. On appeal by special leave, HELD: (i) The Tribunal has failed to notice that in all the awards in recent times in various concerns in Bombay region had the trend been to fixed the age. In most of the cases the age was fixed at 55 and in some cases the trend has been to fixing the date of retirement at 58. [426 D] (ii) The approach adopted by the Tribunal in dealing with this aspect of the problem is not very commendable, and that its present conclusion that what was said by itself on an earlier occasion and was confirmed by this Court in some of its earlier decisions as to how long ago the age should be fix at 60 is incorrect. [427 G] (iii) The trend in Bombay regions was correct. It is clear from the evidence that in many cases the Tribunal had found that in several years in recent occasions the trend was to fix a date of retire ment at 60 but it has not been shown that there was any trend in the matter. In some cases, the trend in Madras region was incorrect and the Tribunal has not given any reason for holding that the prevailing trend had not been correctly fixed. [441 B C] (iv) The fact that in some years in the Bombay region there is a general agreement that the age would be 60 or 58 does not show that it is not correct to say that the rise in Bombay Region was incorrect, is on the whole unsound.

The appellants were directors of a company. The Board of Directors of the company was constituted under section 3(1) of the . The Board, in exercise of its powers under section 237(b), appointed one or more competent persons as inspectors to investigate the affairs of the Company and to report thereon in such manner as the Central Government may direct. The appellants filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the order on the ground that it was passed without jurisdiction because the Board had no power under section 236(b) to delegate its function under section 239(c). The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the Board could not delegate its functions under section 235(b). In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The discretion conferred on the Central Govern ment by section 237 (b) is administrative and it can validly exercise the power of delegation. [322 C] (ii) The power conferred on a Central Government by section 236 (b), to order an investigation and delegated by it to the Company Law Board, is administrative. It could be exercised by the Chairman of the Board only if he was satisfied that there were circumstances suggesting that the business of the appellants was being conducted with intent to defraud its creditors, members or other persons and further that the persons concerned in the management of the affairs had in connection therewith been guilty of fraud, misfeasance and other misconduct towards the company and its members. [321 D E] (iii) The word 'may ' used in section 237 is wide enough to include within its ambit all matters which are necessary for the purpose of carrying out the purposes of the Act. It does not mean that the power conferred by it must be exercised in a reasonable manner or not arbitrarily or capriciously. [323 G] (iv) The words 'may" in section 236 are wide enough and they can only mean 'shall '. There is no doubt that the word 'shall" in the section means 'must '. It cannot be said that the discretion conferred by the statute must be read as a whole or not in a narrow sense so as to include all matters within its scope. [324 C] The word "may" has been used in contradistinction to "may". In other words, he has not disclosed anything from which it can be said to have been exercised by him. It is only when the Board is satisfied that some of these things are necessary that the opinion to be formed under section237(b)(i) should be formed.

The appellants were convicted under section 395 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to 5 years ' rigorous imprisonment and fine. The High Court in appeal set aside their conviction and sentence on the ground that they had been falsely implicated by the dacoits. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The presumption under section 114 of the Evidence Act is not a weak one but it is only when the accused can be connected with the crime. It depends upon the circumstances under which the discovery of the fruits of crime is made immediately after the crime is committed. Disposal of the stolen property or could be placed in the custody of friends till such time as the original offenders could have taken them away. [14 B C] (ii) The time gap between the discovery and the recovery of the articles is not so long as the accused could have known that they were stolen property from some other persons who were prosecuted as offenders. It is only in exceptional cases that the presumption may be drawn. In the present case, the appellants had been rightly convicted by the courts below. [15 C D] (iii) The fact that the appellants were merely receivers of stolen property was not a circumstance which could point to the way as to how the presumption might be drawn and it is legitimate to raise the presumption in this case that the persons with whom the goods were found were the dacoits themselves.

The petitioners are manufacturers of 'thinner ' within Rule 2(x)(2) of the Delhi Poisons Rules, 1926. They were manufacturing 'thinser ' in a mixture containing spirit and other soluble material which contain spirit and also other spoisons. The petitioners contended that the Act was violative of Article 14 of the Constitution inasmuch as it gave arbitrary power to the State Government to include any substance as poison for the purpose of restriction to be imposed on the posses sion for sale and sale of the same. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1.1 The Act is intended to regulate the importation, possession and sale by cattle poisoning or mischief by cattle poison. It is not in dispute that the petitioners were manufacturing "thinerner" within Rule2(x) (2). [222B C] 2.1 Section 5 of the Act deals with presumption and regulated the possi sion of any specified poison in a rule or notification issued under the Act. The Rules of 1926 are made in exercise of the power under section 3 of the , and as such continued in force. [222C D] 2(a) The Act does not deal with any substance other than the substances which may be specified in the rules. It only provides that no person shall sell or otherwise dispose of any poison except in accordance with a licence granted under the Rules. [223F G] (b) The State Government has power to regulate and sale and purchase of poisons. Section 5 deals with the presumption and regulates the poss ion for the sale and the sale of such poison. [225G] 2.(c) The word 'thriner ' in Rule 2 (x)(1) includes a person who is engaged in the business of manufacture, sale or storage of poison. It also provides that any substance which may contain spirit or other sauces mentioned in clause (x) of rule 2 shall be kept in a room or building (according to quantity maintained), which shall be secured by lock and key and in which no sub stance shall be placed other than poisons possessed in accordancewith a licence issued under this Act. [226B C, E] 2:2 The word "thrier" is not defined in the Act but it has been defined in section 2(g) of that Act to mean any substance specified as a poison specified in Rule 1 thereof. It includes substances which are used for the purposes of the act or for the pur pose of the offence. [227D] 3:3 The word `thriers ' is not used in the definition clause but it is used in contradistinction to "another substance". The nature of the substance which is a poison is such that nobody can be considered to have an absolute right to carry on the same, and the notification and its application to any area would depend on the necessity to declare the substance as medicine on the particular facts and situation prevailing in that area and the need to regu sion the substanceas poison on the specific facts and circumstances prevailing in the area.

The assessee firm, a registered under the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, carried on business at Madras in drugs, chemicals, mercury, mercuries, merciless and yam and silk yarn. The assessee firm applied to the Tribunal under section 66(2) of the Indian Incometax Act, for a statement of the case on the following question: "Whether on the facts and in the circumstances of the ease, the Tribunal was right in law in holding that the debt of Rs. 2,68,385/ was not one incurred in the course of business of the assessee ?" The Tribunal rejected the application but held that the amount of Rs,. 2,67,385 was not a bad and doubtful debt in its income which was not an "accommodation" within the meaning of section 10(2)(xi) of Indian Income Tax Act. On appeal by the Revenue to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the Tribunal erred in disallowing the amount claimed by the assessee in its books of account as irrecoverable and (ii) the interest if any charged and a summary of the orders made by the Income tax Officer, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner and the Tribunal were not open to question. HELD : The Tribunal was wrong in disallowing a part of the claim for bad debt. [12 C] In the present case the assessee firm had made no profits or losses in its business. It was only after the receipt of the balance sheet that the monies sent by it to the Bombay firm were not loans made in the ordinary course of its money lending business and the trans actions in the account were totally unconnected with the normal business of its business, nor in respect of any other business of assessee. [13 D E] The Tribunal had found that the moneys sent by the appellant to the Madras firm were in fact loans in the normal course of the money lending trade and the failure to adjust interest in the accounts of the Bombay Firm at the stage which it became a debtor in Samvat year 2007, the manner in which the partner of the firm tried to explain the position in March 1954 and the stand of the partnership firm itself at all earlier stages support the case of the Department.

The petitioners in these cases were owners of certain lands which were acquired by the respondents under the provisions of Section 17 and 19 of the Bangalore Development Act, 1976. The acquisition proceedings lapsed on September 20, 1984. On September 11, 1985, the petitioners obtained an interim order from this Court directing status quo with regard to the possession of the lands in question in Special Leave Petition No. 294 of 1985 preferred against the decision of the Devision Bench of that High Court. The said interim orders were vacated by a Division Bench of the High Court on September 19, 1984 and the appeals filed against the same were dismissed by a Single Judge of that Court on October 6, 1989. In these two writ petitions, the respondents obtained an order of stay of further proceedings in respect of the acquisition of the said lands. The petitioners obtained interim orders from this court directing status of quo with respect to the posses sion of the land in question. On December 16, 1987, the Division Bench granted interim stay of the further proceedings. In the appeals before this Court, it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that as the awards in these two cases had not been made within two years of the making of the declaration under Section 4 of the Land Acquisition Act, they were no longer open to challenge by way of a writ petition. On behalf of respondents it was submitted that as awards in those cases have not been passed within two year of the publication of the declarations under Section 6 of the Act, the entire acquisition proceedings had lapsed and that the award should have been made in accordance with law. Dismissing the petitions, this Court HELD: 1.1 The relief under Article 136 of the Constitution is discretionary and petitioner who approaches this Court for such relief must come with frank and full disclosure of facts. If he fails to do so, his application is liable to be dismissed. [567B] 1.2 In the instant case, the stay orders were highly material in the determination of these Special Leave Petitions. The interim orders have a direct bearing on the question raised and the non disclosure of the same certainly amounts to suppression of material facts. On this ground alone, the Special Leave petitions are liable to he rejected. [568D] 1:3 In view of the provisions contained in Section 11 A of the Acquisition Act read with Rule 11 A(2) of the Rules framed thereunder, the total acquisition proceedings for acqui sition of the appellants lands shall lapse. The award should be made within a period of two years from such commencement. [569E] 1 :4 In view thereof, the interim orders having a direct impact on the issue raised and non disclosure thereof certainly amounts tO to suppression or material facts, their application is required to be rejected. It is well settled in law that the relief under article 136 of tho Constitution is discretion and petitioner which approaches this court for such reliefs must comewith frank and complete disclosure of fact.

The respondent company was incorporated in the United States of America. The award provided that the workmen would be fitted in the new scales of pay from January 1, 1962 on stage adjustment basis i.e., workmen who were drawing basic pay at a particular stage in the time scale of the Sastry award as modified by placing him at the stage in Sastry award equal to, or next above his basic pay as on January 1. 1959. The respondent company filed an application under section 33A of the Industrial Disputes Act before the Central Government for payment of the difference between the basic pay and the basic wage. The Tribunal held that the award was not justified because it was based upon a settlement arrived at by the parties and that the reference was incompetent. On appeal, the High Court set aside the order of the Tribunal and directed the Tribunal to make a fresh award in accordance with law. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The award was invalid as it was not based on any settlement arrived on the basis of the settlement arrived by the respondent company. [901 C] (ii) The Tribunal had no jurisdiction to go into the question whether the award amounted to a settlement or not. It was open to the parties to raise all contentions before it and this Court could not interfere with the order passed by the Tribunal. [951 G H] (iii) The Award was invalid because it did not give any reasons for its conclusion. The Award did not contain any reasons which would justify the inference that the Tribunal had acted without jurisdiction. [952 A B] (iv) The fact that the Sastry Award was given in 1962 and the award in 1962 was signed by the two Arbitrators, did not make any difference because the award provided for a different procedure for determining the basic wages.

The Government of West Bengal, in exercise of its powers under section 3(1) of the West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956, issued a notification dated June 29, 1981 to the effect that the said land was leased out to the Taj Group of Hotels for a period of five years commencing from 1st April, 1981. The Government of India, by a letter dated June 30, 1981 addressed to the Secretary, Animal Husbandary Department, Government of Assam, informed the Zoo that the lease granted to him was for a term of five year and that he would be entitled to continue in possession till the expiry of the said period of ten years. The Zoo was also given notice of termination of the lease by the Government of the land. The lessee filed an application before the Controller of Estate Duty, Calcutta under section 14(1)(a) of West Premises Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948 for eviction of the lessee on the ground that he had failed to pay rent for the period of the expiry. The Controller of Estates Duty held that the lessee was not entitled to any relief in respect of the leased land. He also rejected the application holding that the decision to lease the Begumbari land to the Sta te Hotels was taken on February 12, 1981 and that the Zo was a Garden hotel. The Appellate Authority confirmed the order of eviction. In the writ petition filed by the lessee, the High Court held that there was no evidence to show that the Government had ever made any attempt to evict the lessee and that it was not possible for the lessee to prove that he was in possession of the leasehold land. It also rejected his application holding: (i) that the land which was leased to the Hotel was a garden hotel, and (ii) that there were many chances of the ecology and environment improvement as a result of planting numerous trees all around the proposed hotel and removal of the burial ground and Bird ground for rubbish. The High Court also held that it would be unreasonable to infer that the construction of the hotel in the Begambari land would interfere in any manner with the animals in the Zoological Garden. Allowing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: 1.1 The lease granted by the State Government to the hotel group of Hotels was not a lease by itself and the lessee had no right to sell the same. [263G] 2.1 In the absence of any evidence that the State had made available to it all documents in connection with the proposal for lending over a piece of land, the lease would be wholly inept because in view of the State Policy there would be no question of any resin being sold in the open market would interfere with the animal in the holy hotel. [264A] 2:2 The High Courts were right in holding that there is no evidence on record to show as to how the construction was made by the lessees. The lease deed dated June 28, 1981 was executed between the lessee 's father and the Government. There was nothing to show or even any suggestion that the lessor had ever intended to sell a portion of the plot of land for a price. [265B] 3:3 The lease was not for a fixed period of 10 years. It was only an agreement to sell for a sum of Rs. 1,00,000/ and the lease was for 99 years. There is no material on record that the lessees had ever been making any attempt or even making any effort to get the land sold in their own right. The lessees were not aware of the fact that the leased area was a small garden hotel. They did not have any intention to sell it. [262C D] 4:4 The lease being for 99 year, there is hardly any scope for any inference that the constructions would interfere or otherwise disturb the ecology.

The assessee, a partnership firm, carried on business in cloth and cloth. The Income Tax Officer treated the amount of Rs.67,560/ as income from undisclosed sources and taxed it at Rs.1,50,000/ . On appeal by the assessee, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the sum of Rs,.67,561/ was rightly included in the net wealth of the assessee. In reference under section 27(1) of the Act, the High Court answered the question against the assessee and in favour of the Revenue. The Revenue appealed to this Court. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was in error in answering the question in the manner it did. [129D] 2. The Tribunal had occasion to discuss this aspect in the case of Commissioner of Income Tax, New Delhi vs Ashok Glass Works, there is no warrant for holding that the amount gifted by the donor would not constitute delivery of possession over the gifted property to the donee and gift in such case will not be valid. [130E] 3. The assessee had made a valid gift of Rs 1 lakh and Rs.50, 000 to his son, L and of Rs,50000 made in his favour and credited the same in the personal account of his son. The gift was held to be valid and the amount was rightly taxed at Rs 1,50.000. [131F] 4. The fact that the assessee had paid a sum of RS.67.560/ on 1.1.1957 would not make any difference because the amount in question was not available with the firm or the family or a company which was not a banking company or a banking Company which was neither a banking nor a banking concern. [132G] 5. The mere fact that there was acceptance of the gift by the donee would not effect a valid transfer even though there was an acceptance of that gift by him would not effectuate a valid title. [133A B] 6. In the instant case, the assessee did not make a valid gifts of Rs 50,000 and credited it in the individual account of the firm. The amount was not shown to be income from the undisclosed sources. It was held on the facts that there were no registered deed and as there was no delivery of the property, the gift could not be said to be invalid. [134D] 7.

The appellant, a member of the Orissa High Court Service, was posted as District and Sessions Judge. The State Government by an order dated October 10, 1966 transferred him to the post of District and Session judge. The appellant challenged the orders of transfer before the High Court in a writ petition filed by some of the members of the Subordinate Courts Tribunal. The High Court held that the appellant had no authority to hold the posts in question. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the order transferring the District Judge from one post to another was unsustainable; and (ii) the transfer order was bad because the State Government had not been placed at the disposal of the government for any definite period, it was open to the High court to recall them and post them as presiding officers of district courts. HELD: The High Courts were within its powers in posting Shri B.K. Misra as the law secretary, deputy law and superintendent and legal remembrancer. [626 C] Ranga Mahammad vs S.N. Sinha, ; , followed. (i). The cadre with which we are concerned in this case consists of three parts i.e., (1) presiding officers, district judges and administrative officers working in the secretariat; (2) the Registrar of the High Courts and the administrative tribunal members and administrative members tribunal respectively, on and after October 10 1966, and (3) the judicial officers working at the secretarial department. The cadre is with which the High courts are concerned. [625 D E] Rangas Mahammad 's case ; , referred to. (ii). The High court was within its power in posting one of the district judges already appointed or promoted and posted to the cadre of district judges.

The appellant was the owner of certain agricultural lands in Haryana. He purchased these lands from his vendor and sold them to the respondents. The respondents filed a suit for pre emption against the appellant on the ground that they were co sharers in the said lands. The trial court decreed the suit holding that there was no infringement of Article 19(1)(f) of the Constitution. The High Court dismissed the appeal by the appellant, and hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The object of the Punjab Pre emption Act, 1913 is to provide for the acquisition of rights in agricultural lands and for matters connected therewith. Section 15(1) (b) provides that where the sale is of a share out of joint land or property and is not made by all the co sharer jointly, the right of pre emptption shall vest First, in the son or daughter 's brother or broth er 's sons or daughters of the vendor or vendors; Secondly, in case the sale was of a part out of the joint land, or property sold or a part thereof. Thirdly, in cases where the sales are of a co share 's brothers or the mother 's son or daughters 's father or brother 's husband or sons of the vendors, the rights of preempt shall vest first in the sons or daughter of such female, in their respective shares jointly, and the right to acquire or dispose of property conferred by Article 19 (1) of 'fourthly ' clauses 'Fourthly ' and 'Thirdly '. [127H; 128A B] 1.2 The object underlying the Act is to confer a right on specified persons to pre em ployment in certain circumstances, namely, (a) to acquire rights in land or to dispose of such property; (b), to transfer such lands to others as may be prescribed by the State Government; and (c) to provide that where any sale is made by a co owner jointly with all the other co sharees jointly, each co sharee shall have the right. [128C D] 1(a) The legislature desired to confer the right on certain persons to co shar erers in section 15(i)(b) even if they happen to be co sharors jointly, only the other members jointly, i.e., the brother or the father 's sister or the brothers ' sons of vendor or vendor. [129D] (b). The legislature intended to confer on certain specified persons a right of preemption in respect of agricultural lands. It is clear that the legislature desired that no co sharner should be left out. [130E F] 1.(c) The Legislature wanted to confer an option on specified members of the family of the vendee or vendors in the first three clauses of section 15 (1)(b). [128D] 2(a). It is true that the Legislature desired to give a co tenant a right to preempt from the operation of the Act. But it did not think that there should be any co shar in the land or the property sold by him. The legislature wanted to give such a co tenants a right which conferred a right in respect thereof. [131F] (c).

The petitioner and the second respondent were brothers. They had executed a compromise deed in respect of certain lands in favour of the petitioner and his two sons, in lieu of relinquishment of their interest. The terms of the compromise stipulated payment of Rs. 1 lakh by the father to each of the two sons and the third respondents. In the face of such a statement in the compromise deed signed by the parties, the second Respondent had disputed the fact of payment and has, in the face thereof, accepted the document of compromise to be genuine. The petitioner filed a suit for title and injunction against the second and third respondents, apart from maintaining that his client had not received Rs.1 lakh as stipulated and he had no intention to accept the compromise. The Trial Court dismissed the suit holding that once the Court was satisfied that there were agreements for sale prior to 21.8.1987, the alienees had no interest in the property prior to the compromise and they had accepted the fact that the parties have signed the compromise petition which contain terms which they had accepting and all parties have accepted the documents of compromise, to be real. The second respondent filed an appeal before the High Court against the judgment of the trial court. The High Court dismissed his appeal holding that since the compromise was valid and binding on the alienee, he had taken the stand that the said alienations are valid and the transferees have become owners of the property from the date of the sales which is more than three years old by now. Hence this special leave petition. Allowing the special leave Petition, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High court was in error in holding that the compromise decree was not binding on both the parties. [541G] 1.2 In view of the fact, that there was allegation of payment of RS. 1 lakhs to the alienors, apart form maintaining that their client had also accepted the transaction of compromise and all the parties had accepted it and all parawise the document signed by them, there is no acceptable evidence.

The appellant company was a sick leave. The workmen of the company were paid bonus for the first two days of sickness, and the second day of the spell of sickness for which the sickness benefit was last paid. The company claimed that the benefits of the Employees ' State Insurance Scheme would become available to them under the Act as they were not entitled to the sickness benefits for the second two days. The Industrial Tribunal held that the benefit of sick leave was admissible only in the case of a spell of illness, and that the workmen had no right to claim the benefit for the subsequent two days also. On appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant company that the employees of the Company get the benefit Of 7 days sick leave, and, therefore, they were entitled to receive any similar benefit admissible under the provisions of the Act. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: (1) The Tribunal has not given any reasons for allowing the benefit to the workmen of a sick Leave. [864 D] (2) It is well settled that in industrial adjudication the question whether benefits are granted by the , but that is not a bar to the demand of the workmen for sick leave cannot be categorised as privilege leave, because, it would be admissible only if actual sickness certified by a registered medical practitioner. It is not necessary that in the circumstances of the case, to award the benefit under the first proviso to section 49 of the , that the Tribunal should not, in any view of the matter, have given the benefit on full emoluments during the period of the workman 's physical incapacity to earn his normal wages because of his sickness. [874 D E] (3) The appellant company is entitled to get the benefits admissible under section 49(2)(b) of the . [865 G H] (4) It was not necessary in the facts of the present case to award benefit of the sick leave to the workers on full pay and dearness allowance in 1958, subject to the condition that the total amount of sickness certified as a registered Medical practitioner by a Registered medical practitioner would be Rs. 1,00,000/ . [876 B C] (5) The workmen were not eligible for the benefit claimed by them. They had no other claim except that they should have been granted sick leave at least for the period during which the sick Leave was last payed. [884 E F] (6) It cannot be said that the appellant Company got the benefit from the first day of sickness and, in fact, it did not deal with all aspects of the demand for sickness benefit and did not, at any rate, provide for the grant of leave on full salary during the periods of the worker 's physically incapacity to earning his normal wage because of the sickness. The other question regarding the adequacy of sick Leave is such a leave could not be categorised, as privilege Leave, as by its very nature, it will be admissible in the ease of actual sickness. That was obviously under a mistaken impression of the illness benefit which the Act allowed for, as has been shown, it does not deal all aspects with all aspect of the demands for sickness benefits and does not, At any rate provide for grant of sick leaves on full wages during the first three days also.[864 E G] (7) The argument that the workers were entitled only to the benefit in view of section 49 is without substance. It cannot, therefore be accepted that the claim for sick Leave must be rejected. [854 A B] (8) The contention that the sickness relief could not he denied was untenable because it was not a case of sickness. It was also not necessary to consider whether the benefit could be classified as privilege or leave.

The appellant was detained under section 3(1) of the , by an order dated August 8, 1955 passed by the Government of Bombay. The grounds were not specific and no particulars of the activities alleged to have been carried on by the appellant or made available to the Portuguese Government. The appellant challenged his detention in a petition under article 226 of the Constitution on the ground that the grounds furnished were vague and not bona fide. Held, that the order was bad as it did not disclose any particulars of activities which had been carried out by the detenu. It was not necessary for the appellant to mention these matters in the affidavit filed in the High Court. The fact that at no time it was in public interest to disclose these details does not affect the validity of the order of detention. The question as to whether or not article 22(6) of tile Constitution overrides the constitutional right to be furnished particulars under article 22 (5) to the extent of denying all particulars and leaving the grounds absolutely vague does not arise. It is open to the appellant, if he so chose, to ask for particulars at the time when the grounds were furnished. The failure to mention those matters in his affidavit did not vitiate the order. The decision cannot be said to have hampered his constitutional right of representation and an obligation to communicate it to him. The mere fact that the copy of the grounds was supplied does not invalidate the order as to the mala fides on the part of the detaining authority. The non supply of particulars in a case where no particulars are at all furnished, is not a ground for quashing the order under article 32(1).

The respondent was a commissioned officer in the Army. He was dismissed from service by an order dated April 9, 1959. The appellant filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution for quashing the order of removal from service on the ground that r. 14 of the Army Rules 1954, was ultra vires the , and that the action taken thereunder was without any authority. The High Court held that r, 14 of Army Rules, 1954, had been ultra vires. In appeal to this Court it was contended that r 14 of Defence of India Rules, 1955, which provided for punishment for unbecoming conduct, viz., section 45, was void as it contravened article 311(2) of the constitution and that no action taken under r. 15 could be taken against him without complying with the provisions of section 45. HELD: (i) The two sections 19 and 45 are mutually exclusive. They are mutually independent. [449 B] (ii) Rule 14 is not ultra vires article 14 of tho Constitution. It does not make any difference whether a person has been dismissed or removed from service under r, 16. The two provisions are mutually separate. The first part of section 19(1)(a) gives power to the Central Government to remove or dismiss an officer without being tried and convicted by court martial if he is an officer, subject to the other provisions of the Act and such rules, the Central Govern ment may dismiss or remove from service any person subject to this Act. [451 C] (iii) Rule 15(a) specifically gives power on the Central Govt. to make rules for the purpose of carrying into effect the provisions Of the Act. The second part of that section provides that no order made under r 14 shall be deemed to have been made by any authority subordinate to the Government unless such authority has been given an opportunity to show cause against it. [452 D] (iv) Rule 16(a), which is a rule providing for the removal from serv ice, does not contravene article 311 of the Constitu tion. The words "subject to the provisions" in section 19 are wide enough to include within its ambit all officers who have been dismissed and removed from the service. [453 E] (v) Rule 17(a)(i) gives powers to the appropriate Government to make Rules for the purposes of carrying out the provisions contained therein. The power given to the State Government under section 19 is not unguided or uncanalised. It is, therefore, ultra vires on the grounds that it contravenes article 311. [454 G] (vi) Rule 18(a). which provides for the punishment for misconduct against an officer whose further retention in service is not considered desirable, doesnot contravene article 14. The word "subject" in r.14 of the Rules means something more than what is contemplated by the Act itself. It cannot be said that the words " subject to any of the provisions thereof" occurring in section 18(1) are wide and comprehensive enough to cover all officers belonging to the service except those who have already been dismissed, removed or discharged from service. The expression "subject ' in r 14 is wide enough not only to include all officers but also to all persons who have retired from service as well as those who had already been dis missed or discharged.

The appellant company was carrying on the business of manufacturing tea in its factory. It imported tea from outside the limits of the Panchayat for consumption, use or sale therein and at such rates as may be decided by it but not below the minimum and not exceeding the maximum rates specified in columns 2 and 3 respectively of Schedule 1 annexed to the Rules. The appellant company filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution challenging the legality of the levy on the ground that the Standing Committee had failed to fix the octroi limits in accordance with law, and that the imposition of octroi was invalid as it had failed not fixed the octroi limit in accordance therewith. The High Court held that the Municipality was entitled to deal with the appeal on merits. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The Standing Committee was entitled only to deal With the appeal only on merits, but not beyond the minimum rates specified by columns 2 & 3 of Schedule I annexed to r.22. [222 B] (ii) The High Courts were right in holding that the rules framed under the Act and the Rules relating to the levy of octroi from April 1, 1963, were ultra vires the powers conferred on it by section 5(2)(b) of the Act. [223 C D] (iii) The rule which authorises the levy is r.3 and 4 and is headed "Appeal against levy of any tax or fee" and the period of sixty days commences from the date of publication of the notice under r.4 i.e., the notice which is on the record to show that as a matter of fact the publication was not in accordance by law. Rule 5(1) provides that the Panchayat shall notify to the public not later than one month after the date fixed for the purpose of levying octroi and in such resolution shall specify the rate at which it is to be levied. The rule does not say that the tax shall accordingly be levied from the dates specified in the notice. [225 G H] (iv) Rule 5 provides that if the octroi is not so notified, the Panchayat may levy any tax on the goods imported into the municipal limits of a panchayat. The proviso to rs.3(b) requires that the procedure prescribed in rr. 3 and 4 should be followed before the octroi duty can be levied, but it does not mean that the notice must be published by affixing a copy thereof in the office of the panchayat. [226 B C] (v) Rule 4 is intended to give effect to the provisions of r. 5(3). The rule requires that every Panchayat shall publish a notice in the manner prescribed in r. 3. The notice should also contain a statement showing the rate of octroi and the date on which it was to be collected.

The appellants were convicted under section 31(1) read with section 33 of the , and sentenced to a fine of Rs. 5,000/ . The appellants contended that as conciliation proceedings had continued for more than 14 days as from January 17, 1952, further proceedings for conciliation were illegal and therefore the accused persons could not be convicted under s.31(1). Held, that the conciliation proceedings should be held to terminate when the report of the Conciliation Officer is received by the appropriate Government. The conciliation proceedings are deemed to have concluded in the case where no settlement is arrived at, when the Report of the Board is published under section 17, as the case may be; and if the conciliation proceeding were not closed but were carried on, as they were in the present case, the termination of the conciliation Proceedings would depend upon how soon a report is received. The provisions of the Act do not contemplate that the report should be made and the proceedings closed within a fortnight and if proceedings are not closed within 14 days he may be guilty of a breach of duty but in law the proceedings do not automatically come to an end after 14 days but only terminate as provided in section 20(2)(b) of the . The conciliation proceeding under section 20 is deemed to take place when the reports of the Boards are received by it and that report is made within 14 months. The appellants were rightly convicted under sections 31(i), 31(2) and 33 of Act. Held, further, that as the conciliation proceeds had continued beyond 14 days the dismissal could not he said to be one within the words " pendency of conciliation proceedings".

The petitioner was detained under section 3(2) of the . The District Magistrate, Dhanbad in respect of the petitioner 's activities, was satisfied that his release from detention was imminent and the order of detention was necessary for putting him back in jail. The petitioner challenged the order on the ground that the detaining authority had confirmed the order and therefore it could not be said that there was any real danger of his release. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1. The grounds for forming the satisfaction of the detaining authorities were properly considered by the detaining authori ties while passing the detention order. [910G] Rameshwar Shaw vs District Magistrate Etah and others ; , followed. Rameshwar Shaw v District Magistrate Dhanbad & Anr., ; Ramesh Yadav vs District Magis trate, Burdwan & Anr. ; ; Ramesh Yahan vs District magistrate Etah and Ors., ; ; Rameshwar Shaw V. District Magistrate , Burdwan & Ors., AIR 1974 SC 2261; Rameshwar Shaw & Anr vs District Collector Etah and Others, ; ; Ram Krishna Shaw vs State of West Bengal, ; and Rameshwar Shaw 's case, referred to. 2. The detaining authority while passing an order of deten tion under section 8(2), has not applied his mind properly to the relevant material on record. It is only when the subjective satisfaction of that authority was reached that it can be said to have been arrived at by the authority in a reasonable manner. [ 907D E] Rameshwar vs District authori ty, Burdwan and Anr., AIR 1975 SC 2262; Rameshwar Ghosh vs District Judge Etah & Ors. ; , referred to and distinguished. In the instant case when the actual order of the detention was served upon the detenu, the detenu was in jail and was likely to be enlarged on bail. Therefore, though the order was passed at the time of the service of the order there was no proper consideration of the fact that the detenu had since been released or that the prospect of his imminent release was properly considered before the detaining au thority properly and seriously before the service.

The appellant company was engaged in gold trade and in the manufacture of gold ornaments. The company had its registered office at Hyderabad. In the year 1973, it sold gold to various dealers in Bombay. The sales were effected by the company in Bombay and the sale proceeds were credited to the account of the company. The appellant company filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of section 28 of the Gold Control Act, 1968 on the ground that it suffered from the vice of excessive delegation of legislative power inasmuch as no criteria or guide lines have been laid down by reference to which the power conferred upon him thereunder could be exercised and that the section confers an arbitrary and uncanalised power without any criteria or guidelines for guiding the Administrator in the matter of exercising his discretion under section 5(1) of the Act. The High Court struck down the aforesaid provision only on the grounds that it suffers from the lack of excessive delegated legislative power and its validity has to be upheld. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant company that (i) the restrictions imposed by the section were unreasonable and violative of article 19(1)(g) of Constitution; (ii) the restriction in the case of a third person in carrying on money lending business not to be carried on in licensed premises was not absolute as much as the Administrator could authorise the third person to carry on the business in gold, ornaments and articles of gold and articles thereof; and (iii) the provisions of section 5 of the were violative of Article 19(6). Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The power conferred on the Administrator under section 28 by reference is not absolute in as much the Administrator can authorise the second person to carrying on business as a money lender, banker or any other business in the same premises. [954F] 2. Section 28 confers an unguided and uncanized power without anything criteria or guidance lines having been put on the activities of the traders doing business in Gold will have to be viewed from the aforesaid perspective. The object of the enactment and the scheme affords sufficient guidance to Administrator in matters of exercising the discretion conferred on him under section5(1). [955G] 3.

The appellants filed a suit against the respondents for possession of certain properties on the ground that they were entitled to the possession of the properties. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court reversed it holding that the title of the alienees in regard to 'maddharlayam properties had not been lost by adverse possession before the suit was filed. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The transfer made by the manager of a Hindu endowment on the basis that it belonged to the religious endowment is challenged by his successor on the grounds that it belongs to him and not to the temple. If such a claim was made by respondents 1 to 3 on the date when they were appointed trustees by respondent No. 3, the transfer being void ab initio, the possession had been acquired by adverse posses sion of the transferee from the very beginning and the succeeding manager 's right to challenge the said transfer would be lost if his predecessor who made the transfer lives for more than 12 years after effecting the transfer. [422 D E] (ii) The High Court was in error in reversing the decisions of the courts below by holding that title of 'mad purselayam property had not be lost by respondents I to 3 because they were not holding the same as managers of the trust. [427 G] (iii) The question whether a transfer effected by the Manager of a religious endowment on a proper consideration is void abitio, with the result that possession of a transferee is adverse to the spiritual endowment from the beginning and, the succeeding Manager 's rights to challenge such a transfer would not be affected by the provisions of article 134 B. [409 C] (iv) The contention that the transfer was for valuable consideration cannot be accepted. It is open to doubt whether the said decision could lead to the inference that if a part of the property is transferred by the managers of a temple in regard tO the properties belonging to the denomination, but on the foundation that it belong to the Hindu religious endowment, the transfers are void abso initio. [411 D E].

The appellant firm, a partnership firm, was granted a licence for the Theatre. The license was renewed by the District Magistrate in favour of the firm Apsara Theatre. On April 27, 1979, a suit was instituted against the partners of the Firm Apsar Theatre alleging that the Cinema licence had been granted to them without any authority or jurisdiction and that they were not entitled to be heard before the expiry of the period of license. The District Magistrate rejected the said application on the ground that it had become impossible for him to operate the cinema theatre in view of the temporary injunction issued by the State Government and since it was only the licensee who was held responsible under the Act and Rules for due compliance with all the terms and conditions of the licence, he could not be prosecuted. The appellant 's writ petition challenging the said order was dismissed by a Single Judge of the High Court. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the District Magis trate had no jurisdiction to suspend the licence; and (ii) the impugned order was void as it was passed without notice or hearing the licensee. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The order passed by the Chief Justice directing the suspension of cinema shows in the Theatre cannot be said to have visited the writ petitioners with any adverse civil consequences. [577G] 2. Apsakara Theatre is being conducted by some persons other than the licensee and there is no mention at all of the partnership firm or its partners. An application filed by a partner for renewal of the license in his individual capacity or as representing the partnership cannot be treated as licensees of the Theatre unless the conditions precedent mentioned in the said section are present, the licensing authority had no power under the statute or the Rules to make such an order. [578A B] 3. The impugned order passed was void and in violation of the principles of natural justice. [579C D] 4. A reading of the order passed on September 26, 1980 shows that it was made clear that the District magistrate had no authority to suspend a licence. The licensing authority has no power to suspend or revoke the licence. [580D E] 5. The State Government had issued an order dated December 29, 1977 under section 6 F of the Act authorising the District Collector to suspend cinema for a period of three years from the date of suspension and until such time as he was satisfied that the licensee has been guilty of any act or omission which is prejudicial to the interest of the public, he may be suspended. [581E] 6. The power to cancel or suspend a license is conferred only by section 6F of the . The District Magistra trate has no jurisdiction under the provisions of the , and Rules to made such an ordi natory order. He had no such power in the matter. [576G H] 7.
