The High Court was not right in quashing the impugned orders passed by him.

The appellants were lessees of certain mills situated in Pakistan. They applied for a lease of the mills under section 12 of the , and the respondent was granted a lease by the Custodian, but the appellants refused to do so. The respondent filed an application before the Custodian for cancellation of the lease on the ground that the appellants had failed to comply with the terms of the leases and that the Custodian had no authority to issue the notice in question under section 10 of the Act. The Custodian rejected the application. On appeal, the Additional District Judge held that the provisions of section 12 applied only to leases granted by the evacuee and not by the respondent himself and that no directions could be given under section 13 of the . He further held that section 12 was applicable only to transfers made by the evacuees but not by others. The appellants came up in appeal to this Court with certificate granted by this Court. Held, that the words "notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force" in section 12(1) of the were wide enough to cover all transfers made under the Act and that section was applicable even to leases made by evacueees but also by others and not to leases which were made by them. The provisions of sections 12 and 13 of Act did not apply to leases executed by evacents in respect of property belonging to evacuee, and the appellants could not be allowed to challenge the validity of the notice under section 8(1). Held further, that section 10 applied only when there was a lease and that it was not necessary for the Custodian to issue any directions with reference thereto. The words " notwithstanding anything contained elsewhere in any law for time being In force" were wide and unqualified and could not have been restricted by reference to the provisions that it could be exercised "notwithstanding any other Law for the lime being in operation".

The appellant was a minor son of Raghubir Singh. He filed a revision application under section 230 of the Rajasthan Land Revenue Act, 1954 before the Board of Revenue for setting aside that part of the Sub Divisional Officer 's order which had gone against the State and in his favour. The Board of revenue set aside the order of the sub Divisional Officer on 5th May 1976 holding that Surendrapal Singh was born to Raghubir Singh on 14th March 1963 and was only 13 years when the ceiling proceedings were finalised by the Sub Divi sion Officer on May 5, 1976. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the said order of Board of Reve nue. The Single Judge allowed the writ petition holding that the Board had no jurisdiction to set aside that portion of the order which was passed against the appellant and in favour of the State. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the State having not filed an appeal under section 225 of the Act of 1955 before the Revenue Appellate Authority, the Board could not review its earlier order; (ii) the Board having appellate jurisdiction and it could not make use of its powers of superintendence and control over subordinate revenue courts and it did not apply to judicial proceedings. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding that it was not appropriate for the Board to exercise the powers conferred by section 9 of the Land Revenue act, 1955. [728G] 2. Section 221 of the Code of Civil Procedure is not subject to the other provisions of the statute. It is clear from the language of Section 221 that the board of Revenue has general power of superintendence over all revenue courts. In the Government of India Act of 1935 there was provision under section 224 for superintendence by the High Courts, but sub section (2) made it clear that this superintendence would not be construed as giving to the High court any jurisdiction to question any judgment of any inferior court which was not otherwise subject to appeal or revision. [700A B] 3. The Government of Indian India Act, 1915 and there is no like section 224 of the Government Act of India, 1915 make it clear from language of section 221 that this control would not he construed as conferring jurisdiction on the High courts to question the orders of subordinate tribunals which were not otherwise subjects to appeal. [628D] 4. The word 'jurisdiction ' in sub section(2) of Section 224 of 1955 is wide enough to include all judicial proceedings and it does not cover judicial proceedings, but only includes administrative or judicial proceedings; it does cover judicial proceeding. It does not include judicial proceedings as well. It merely means judicial proceedings which are quasi criminal. [771B C] 5.

The appellant, a newspaper publisher of the newspaper, was appointed as an officer in charge of the printing press. The first respondent, who was working as a editor of a newspaper, filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the Act and the Rules framed thereunder on the ground that the Act did not contain any news item nor did it contain any newspaper. The High Court accepted the plea of the Ist respondent and declared that the law reports were not newspapers within the meaning of section 2(b) of the Working Journalists (Conditions of Service) and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1955 and that the demand made by the Deputy Labour Commissioner to comply with the order made by him on the basis of the recommendations of Justice Palekar was unsustainable. The appellant contended before this Court that the Bengal Acts which were published by the Ist Respondent were not newspaper within the definition of 'newspaper ' in the Act, and that it was not essential for a newspaper to conform strictly to the usual pattern of a daily or weekly newspaper or monthly newspaper or a magazine containing newspapers. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The law reports published by Ist respondent contain information about recent events which have taken place in the Supreme Court or in the High Courts which are public bodies and these matters in which the public is interested. They are matters in Which the public are public body and those matters in whose favour the Act is passed has to be accepted. [787B] 2. The Act in question is a beneficent legislation which is enacted for the purpose of improving the conditions of service of the employees of newspaper establishments and hence even if it is possible to have two opinions on the construction of the provisions of the statute, one which advances the object of the legislation which was enacted for improving the condition of service. [789C] 3. The expression 'newpaper ' as defined in the Working journalists (Regulation of Service), Miscellaneous Provisions and Miscellaneous provisions Act, 1956 is a beneficial legislation which seeks to improve the conditions and conditions of the service of employees of the newspapers establishments and therefore even if the publication of these items by itself may not occupy a substantial part of a law report to make it a newspaper there is no need for the Legislature of the State to levy sales tax on the sale of any newspaper which may after some time cease to be a newspaper. [788F G] 4. The Bengal Acts in question are not legislation within the ambit of section 3(b). They are not laws made by Parliament and they are not law made by an authority or court. They do not come within the purview of the expression 'public interest ' as used in section 2 (b) and therefore, the Act cannot be said to contain any article so as to become newspaper. It is significant that the expression `news paper ' as understood in the Press and Registration of Books Act, 1867, the Indian Post Offices Act, 1898, the English Post Office Act, 1932, the Orissa Gazette of India which was the official publication of all kinds of news and information was a newspaper within meaning of Section 2(c) of that Act. [ 787A B] 5. The Law reports published in the law Reports which are being published by first respondent contain Information about recent incidents which have take place in Supreme Court and of the High courts which are Public bodies and those matter in which public is interest.

The respondent was a tenant of the appellant. The agreement was described as an agreement of 'leave and licence ' entered into between the parties on the one hand and the appellant on the other wherein the respondent had been described as the licensee and the appel lant had been given and granted his 'leav and licence to use and occupy the said premises for the period of five years. The period of leave and licence was to commence from 1st September, 1965 till 31st August, 1970 and it was stated that the licensor was seized and possessed of and was otherwise entitled as the monthly tenant of a workshop premises situated at 231 Ripon Road, Co operative Building, Bombay. The respondent filed an application for eviction under section 14(1)(e) of the Maharashtra Rent Control Act, 1958 on the ground that he had been in occupation of the premises on 1st February, 1973 under a subsisting agreement for leave and license entered into with the licensor for a period of 5 years from 1 st September 1965 till 30th August, 1969. The Small Causes Court rejected the contention of the respondent holding that the appellant was not a licensee and that he was a sub tenant. The High Court allowed the revision on the view that the respondent was in occupation as a monthly tenant and had found him to be a licensee. In appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that the agreement was a lease and not a licence, and that the landlord could not terminate the tenancy after 31st March, 1966 when there was nothing on record to show that after 31 st March 1966 the respondent 's licence was renewed or any fresh agreement was entered into. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The appellant was a licensee under an agreement with a licensor for 5 years and had agreed to allow him to use the premises under the said leave and Licence agreement between the licensor and the licensor. [21C] 2.1 In view of the language of the document and the background of the entire document, it is clear that the parties were in occupation at the relevant time when the agreement came into force. The document was not an agreement for licence but as a lease. It was a licence and not an interest in the property. [22D] 2:2.

The appellant company was incorporated in the State of Rajasthan under the Rajasthan Merged Territories and Areas (Jagirs Abolition) Act, 1950. The Ruler of the former Jodhpur State became the Ruler of that State on January 26, 1950, and the appellant company became the successor to the former State of Jodhpur. In 1951, the appellant Company made a declaration under article 295(2) of the Constitution in respect of the obligations of the latter State to pay tax on its sales effected by it during the period from April 1, 1948, to March 31, 1950; and the liability of the appellant was limited to the amount of tax collected in advance for the period between April 1. 1948 to March 30, 1951. The appellant company claimed that the liability to pay sales tax under article 294(2), of the constitution, as it stood at the relevant time, was not discharged by the State and its liability to refund the amount was not made on the basis of any agreement between the Ruler and the former. Held: (i) that the appellant had no authority to levy sales tax on the sale effected by the former ruler of Jodhpur State in respect Of the obligations which it had undertaken to pay under the agreement with the latter, and that the new State continued to exist till they were repealed or altered; (ii) that article VI of the Covenant did not confer any right on the appellant as against the new sovereign as it was part of the covenanting State till such time as they were modified by the new state of Rajasthan. The agreement in question was not a law within the competence of the State Legislature and did not transgress the constitutional limitations after the Constitution came into force; (iii) that section 3(1) of Act 1 of 1951, which provided for the continuance of laws in the covenanted State till it came into existence, did not offend article 295 (2); (iv) that there was always recognition by the old sovereign of the existing rights of the residents of those territories and that such a law must prevail and in the presence of such a statute there could be no question of recognition by any new sovereign; (v) that in view of the fact that the Ruler had recognised the liability, the new ruler ceased to exist and the liabilities assumed all liabilities arising from the existence of those laws.

The appellants were carrying on business in the manufacture of commercial crops. They purchased from the market a large quantity of agricultural produce and sold it to others. The State Government declared them as 'a notified area ' under section 4 A of the Act. The appellants challenged the validity of the notification by a writ petition before the High Court. The High Court held that the notification was bad because the market committee did not name the allowance or taking them out of the pro hibition under section 14 which prohibited the deduction of trade allowance and did not operate upon any other payments made which were not trade allowances. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The notification was valid because it did not mention the allowance in any transaction that was being made by the market committees. It merely stated that the committee did so. [109 F] (ii) The High court was wrong in holding that the appellants were not prevented from doing their business and that they were not prohibited from holding the market as property, i.e., the market. [110 B C] (iii) The contention that the market Committee did not include the allowance under section 5 of the Madras General Sales Tax Act is without substance. It was open to the appellants to contend that the Market Committee did so because it had no name or allowance in respect of commercial crop. [111 D E] (iv) The word 'trade allowance ' in section 14(1)(d) means a trade allowance. The word "trade allowance" in section 2(g) means any payment made by way of wages, reward or otherwise to the employees for the work done by them. It is not necessary that the word "business allowance" should be given its ordinary meaning.

The appellants were convicted by the Sessions Judge under section 302 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death. The High Court confirmed their conviction but reduced the sentence to transportation for life. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that : (1) the High Court erred in holding that the appellants were not guilty because they had joined in the attack and so there was no evidence to show that they knew the assailants; (2) the Sessions judge had wrongly convicted the appellants under section 304 Part I of the Code of Criminal Procedure. HELD: (i) The facts disclosed do not warrant an inference of common intention in Pandurang 's case. That leaves the question of sentence in the case of Bhilia and Tukia. It is not necessary that each one must know what he actually joined in it, but that does not mean that every one who knew what he was doing was guilty of the offence. [431 C] (ii) The fact that two or more persons were involved in the crime did not make any difference because they were not present at the scene of occurrence and there was nothing to show as to how many of them actually joined together. There is no reason why the High Courts should not have convicted the appellant under section 326, Part I, Code of criminal Procedure. [427 E] (iii) The circumstances disclosed do indicate that the two accused were present at a particular place and they had come to know of it only when some one was present. There was also evidence that all three lived together and that one was a younger brother and the other tenant of the appellant in question. There could be no doubt that there was some vague evidence to the effect that there had been once a dacoity at Ramchander 's house and that he suspected "the accused" and that they must have joined in those attack but nothing came of it and they were later released.

The petitioner in the two writ applications under Article 32 of the Constitution was employed as an engineer in the Central Public Works Department under the Ministry of Works and Housing. He was compulsorily retired by order dated 3.8.1976 with effect from 5.11.76 on the ground that he attained the age of 50 years on 10.2.1972 and, therefore, on the date of his compulsory retirement he had completed the age Of 50 years. The petitioner in these two writ petitions under Article 226 challenged the said order by means of a writ petition before this Court contending that the order for retirement was bad as it was passed without complying with the principles of natural justice inasmuch as the petitioner had not attained the minimum age of 55 years on the appointed day and, consequently, he was entitled to draw upto the normal date of superannuation. The respondents in the other two writ peti tions contended that the petitioner was not entitled to any salary for the period of his service and that the impugned order was bad because it was issued without complying the principles laid down by this Court in Tahiliani 's case. Dismissing the writ petitions, ^ HELD: 1. The object of Fundamental Rules 56(j) is to classify Gov ernment servants into two categories and sub clause (i) takes within its sweep those Government servants who at the relevant time are in Class I or Class II service or post on substantive basis. [628D] 2.1 Sub clause (ii) does not apply to Government servants in Class 1 or Class 11 service or posts even when he holds a post of either class substantively or temporarily on officiating basis. The purpose behind it is to classified Gov erned servants into three categories and subsection (i). If the officia is not brought to an end by reverting the Government servant to his substantive post before the power of compul sation retirement is exercised, the Government Servant in Class II or Class I service or Class III service or Post on substantive, temporary or officiating basis has to be retired compulsorily. [625E F] 2(ii) The purpose of Fundamental Rule 56(i) is that classification of Government servants into one category and sub cl.(ii) takes in within its fold those Government servant who at that relevant time were in Class III or Class Il service or cadre on substantive or temporary basis.

The appellant Corporation was a company registered under the Companies Act. It entered into an insurance contract with the respondent Corporation for the purpose of carrying on its business in the city of Bangalore. The policy provided that the premium payable by the deceased would be paid to the Corporation at the time of the death of the deceased and the premium amount would be deducted from the monthly premium payable to the company. The appellant Corporation had duly appropriated the amount and credited in the accounts towards the premium due by it in its accounts and the said premium amount was received by the Corporation without any demur or qualification and that in any event the Corporation must be deemed to have waived by its conduct the formality, if any, formality, whether of sending a communication of its acceptance of the proposal or not. The respondent Corporation had also issued notices to the appellant Corporation demanding payment of the first premium and also for the second premium. The Corporation filed a suit against the appellant in the High Court for recovery of the amount due from the deceased. The trial court decreed the suit but the High court reversed it holding that there was no concluded contract between the deceased respondent and the Corporation and that the proposal sent by the appellant was not accepted and as such there was concluded insurance contract between them. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the first premiums were received by it completely on 11th January 1961 being the date of receipt of the balance towards premium by the corporation; (ii) the Corporation had encashed the cheques issued towards the first and later on 11 1 1961 being a fact which was not established and even if such a representation was made, that did not alter the position as under the rules; (iii) the third premium was received only after 11th of January 1961 but it was also appropriated by it with its accounts, and the amount was not calculated. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was in error in coming to the conclusion that there had been concluded contract of insurance between the appellant and the respondent corporation. [359B] 2.1 The High court was right in holding that the Corporation was the only authority to accept the proposal if it was not otherwise accepted. [360C D] 2(a) In the instant case, the first three premiums were admittedly received by respondent No. 1 on 11 January 1961 and the third was paid on 11rd January 1961. The first premium was not only received by Corporation completely on November 11, 1961 but also appropriated it in the account of the Corporation. [361E] (b) The High Courts were right in taking the view that having regard to the conduct of the parties there was a concluded contract. The finding of the trial court that there is no concluded insurance contracts between the respondent and Corporation cannot be sustained. [362F G] 2.(a) The first premiums received by Respondent No.1 were admittedly not received by them completely on the 11th and 12th January, 1961. It was also accepted that the deceased had paid the first instalment of premium to the corporation. The fact that the first two premiums were paid in advance did not affect the position of law as under Rule 13 of the General Conditions of Contract of Insurance (General Conditions of Insurance) Rules, 1960. [363F G; 363A] 2:2 In the present case, there was an acceptance of proposal by the respondent No 1 and the appellant had also accepted the proposal. The contract of Insurance was complete and offer by the local agent and field officer of the field officer and the field officers of the respondent State Corporation. There was no such acceptance of insurance proposal if the proposal was not considered, that does not alter or change the position under the Rules.

The appellant company was incorporated in the State of Madras. The respondent, a company, was incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913 and its registered office at Madras was situated in Madras. It had its registered Office at Madras. In the course of its business it used to carry on the business of manufacturing and selling textiles. Its principal object was to manufacture textile products and sell them in India. The appellant company had its head office at Calcutta. It used to manufacture and sale textile products. Its head office was situated at Madras, and its head Office was situate at Madras and its Head Office was situated outside Madras. On the question whether the order of the High Court amounted to a judgment or an interlocutory order within the meaning of article 133(1)(a) of the Constitution, HELD: (i) The word "final" in section 205 of the Government of India Act, 1935 means final adjudication by the court of law and not final. [857 D] (ii) An order which is essentially an interlocutory one may be deemed final for the purposes of article 134(1) (c) if it amounts to final decision on the rights of parties in a suit or proceeding from which appeal has arisen, is not final within the scope of article 136(1). [858 E] Mohammad Amin Brothers ' case ; and Mohammad Amin Bros. vs Benaras Bank Ltd., , referred to. (iii) The expression "final order" in article 133 (1) means final determination by the Court of law. It does not mean final decision. It is only when a final decision is rendered that it becomes necessary to decide whether the final order should be made or not. [586 G] Mohammad Anwar Amin Bros., vs Benares Bank Ltd. , referred, to.

The petitioners are manufacturers of grey cloth. They were manufacturing grey cloth in the hands of the processor and selling them to the processor. The processor 's factory alongwith his profit was manufacturing grey fabrics. The petitioners filed writ petitions before this Court for clarification of the judgment dated 4th November, 1988. Dismissing the petition, this Court, HELD: 1. The assessable value of the processed fabric would be the value of that cloth plus the value thereof. If the trader entrusts or cotton man made fabric to the processing for processing on job work basis, would give a declaration to the buyer as to what would be his price at which he would be selling the processed goods in the market, that would be taken by the Excise authorities as the assessable value. [346G H] 2. The expression "deemed factory" is used in Rule 174 of the Central Excise Rules 1944 and it is not necessary to include the processor ' sessable value. If a trader entrusting or cottonman making fabric to him for processing, on job basis, he would give declaration to that processor as to how he would sell the processed fabrics and excise duty would be charged to the manufacturer on that basis provided that the declaration as to the price atwhich he would he was selling the grey cloth or fabric plus the valuation of the job work done plus manufac turing profit and expenses. That would be, the correct as sessage at which the processed cloth would leave the processor factory with his profit and expense. [347B C] 3. The price at Which the processed cotton fabric would leave him with his profits and expenses is the correct price as to which he will be selling it on that date provided that declaration as regards the price of the grey fabrics plus manen turing profits and expense is made by the processor himself. If, however, the value would include only the price or deemed price at the factory gate for processing the processed yarn, then in such a case the value will be Rs.30, being the value or deemed to be the price on which the grey fabric would go into the factory plus his profit. [345D E] 4. The manufacturer of grey fabrics would not have the option to sell the grey cotton fabrics and would have the right to sell it at a higher price. If he entrusts the goods with his own profit and costs, then he would have no option but to sell them at a lower price. [344E F] 5. The value of grey fabric or fabric with the value as to whether the processed product would be sold in the factory or deemed as the price to be paid on that method provided that it is the price which he selling the said goods and the person so authorised agrees to discharge all the liabilities under the said Act and the rules made thereunder. [349C] 6. The cost of processing would include the value added by the process of processing. If there is no such thing, then the manufacturer who entrusts his or cotton fabric with his intention to sell would be entitled to sell at a lesser price. In order to explain the position it is made clear that the assessable values of the processing would be determined on that foundation provided that in case the declared value as the cost of the raw material or the manufacturing profit and the manufacturing expenses are not ascertainable, then only in such cases the value shall be taken as the wholesale price at what he would get. [348D E; 349A] 7. The fact that the processed textile fabric was sold by the petitioner to the processors for processing would not make any difference because it is a case of sale of grey yarn and the cost incurred in processing would also include the manufacturing cost of raw material. [350B C, F] 8. The Tribunal has rightly held that the value declared by the petitioners as the basis of the assessable price of processed fabric should be the same as the value at which they were selling the manufactured goods. [ 349E] 9.

The appellant was appointed as a clerk by the Gram Panchayat, Loharu. On March 14, 1975 he was promoted as Head Clerk on an ad hoc basis in January 1974 and was confirmed in that post in April 1975. He filed a writ petition in the High Court of Punjab and Haryana asking that he should be absorbed as a Head Clerk. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the appellant was entitled to continue in service as a peon in any event. In appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellant that by reason of section 14(4) of the Amending Act, 1973 the Panchayat Samiti lost its power to make appointments to the Panchayats and that the amendment introduced by section 14 of the amending Act of 1973 was not retrospective in operation. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The right to be considered for promotion is a term and condition of service, what is relevant for our purpose is whether the appellant is entitled to be absorbed in Government service as an clerk in any circumstance. [737B] 2.1 The right of the appellant to be included in the Government service was not a term of his appointment but a condition of his service. It could not, therefore, have been appointed as Head Clerks prior to June 13, 1973 when the Amending act came into force. [ 737C D] 2:2. The appellant was not entitled to any benefit of the amendment made in section 14 (4) by the Amending Acts of 1973 and 1974. [ 738E F] 3.1 In view of the deletion of section 33 of the Punjab Panchayat Samitis and Zilla Parishads Act, 1961, the appellant could not have been absorbed as Head clerk on April 1, 1975. [ 735B C] 2 :3. The fact that the appointment was made after June 13 1973 when it purported to do so cannot improve his position for the simple reason that these appointments were made after July 13, 1974 when the amending act came in force. There is no substance in this contention. Even assuming for the purposes of argument that the right to appoint him to the post of Head Clerk had been recognised and protected, despite the fact that such appointment was done after June13, 1973, when the Amendment Act came into effect, he could not be absorbed or a Head clerk without the authority of law. [ 736E F; 737A] 2(a) The appellant 's appointment as a head clerk prior to his absorption in Government Service had to be recognised and saved despite the existence of such appointment. [ 734B C]. (b) The fact, that the post in which the Government has absorbed him was lawfully appointed to the said post by the Panchayat Samitis until he was absorbed in government service had to he recognised and preserved, despite his fact that it was made before June 13. 1973 when he was absorption in government Service had no significance.

The appellants filed a suit for declaration and possession of the properties in dispute. The trial court decreed the suit but on appeal, the High Court reversed the decree. In second appeal to this Court it was contended that the property belonged to the Math or the deity and not to the deity. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) A nucleus of dedicated property exists when the Mahant is succeeded by his predecessor Shivshankar Yati. The property in dispute is a personal property of the Math and therefore a claim to exemption from the levy was made. [663C] (2) The High Court was right in holding that the Amauli properties were acquired by the Mahant only for the purpose of escaping personal liability to tax. [665F] (3) A Hindu died leaving behind his widow, the appellant and his son. The succession certificate issued by the District Judge, against the declaration that the deity was the personal property belonging to the Mahant, was not a regularly constituted Mahant of Math Sauna or of the deity, but only for purposes of escaping liability to pay tax. The High court was right, in the view that the endowment properties were not personal property and they did not belong to the religious or deity. [664H] (4) A religious institution is not an individual or a Hindu. It is a body corporate. Its head office is distinct from its own property. It consists of two separate branches: one branch, the other branch being the principal office of the family. The other branch is the principal place of the principal and the other branches are the principal offices of the members of the public.

The appellants who were displaced persons from West Pakistan, filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution challenging the validity of the order of allotment in their favour by the Custodian General. The Custodian held that the appellants had failed to establish that they had been allotted quasi permanent allotments in their respective villages and that the notification issued thereunder was illegal. The appellants then moved the High Court under article 227 of the constitution for quashing the order on the ground that the Custodian had no jurisdiction to revise the order. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the power of revision conferred by section 19(1) of the Act was not exhausted as the notification was issued in accordance with the provisions of the , and that it was not open to the Custodian to revise his own order. Held, that the order passed by the High court was correct and must be set aside. The words "any other sufficient reason" in section 19 of the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, are wide enough to include any one or more reasons which may be recorded in writing for cancelling an allotment or lease made in favour of a person or to cancel an allotment in the matter of cancellation of an allotment. The power of the Custodian under section 10 of the is not exhausted merely because the property vests in him. The result of the provisions contained in sections 12(2) and 19 of Act is that the evacuee property vested in the Central Government free from all encumbrances. The notification issued by the Central Govern ment under section 12(1), therefore, cannot be said to have been issued without jurisdiction.

The Uttar Pradesh Public Service Commission invited applications from eligible candidates for the post of Upper Zila Basic Shiksha Adhikari (Women) DistrictNE of Girls Schools/Associate Regional Inspectress of Girls School in Uttar Pradesh Educational Service Junior Scale (emale 's Branch). The advertisement inviting applica tion from candidates was published on May 5, 1985 and a corrigendum was published in June 8, 1985. The recruitment examination was in two stages written and written. After the written examina tion was over, on the basis of the results thereof, the Public Service Com mission decided to cancel the entire recruitment examination and asked for a fresh interview of all eligible candidates on the ground that the result thereof had been delayed. In the meanwhile, the State Government issued an advertisement inviting applications from candidates who were eligible for the posts of Upper Basic Shiksha Advi sion (Women 's branch) in Uttar Haryana Educational Service. The advertisement was published by the Public Services Commission on May 6, 1985, and a notification was published as required under Rule 3(1)(a) of the U.P. State Government Service Rules, 1951. The appellants who were candidates for appointment to the post applied for the same. They were called for interview but could not be selected because they had better performance in the written examination. The Public Service commission decided to cancelled the entire selection and asked the candidates to appear before the Selection Committee on account of improper feeding into some of the candidates who had better merit in the viva voce. The State Government, however, did not accept their request. In a writ petition filed by the appellants challenging the validity of the notification, the High Court upheld the action of the Public Com mission and directed that the order of the Commission cancelling the entire recruit ment examination be set aside. Allowing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Public Services Commis sioner was right in holding that when no defect was pointed out in regard to the written part of the recruitment examina tions and drive the candidates for litigation, it was factually estab lished that the Public service Commission decided to cancellation the entire ap pointment examination. [126B] 1.2 The State Public Service Commissions should have been more careful in dealing with the matter so that four years in the process of recruitment would not have been lost and the public would not suffer if public time would not had suffered. It is, therefore, directed that a fresh selection be made by completing the interview examination within four months hence. [127C D] 1.(a) The Public service Commis mission should have more careful dealing with matters so that 4 years in process of recruit ment would not be disturbed. [128D E] (b) The State public Service Commission should have very careful dealing in the matter, so that the four years period in the processes of recruitment will not have suffered public time. [129E F] (c) The selection of two Scheduled Caste candidates and five Backward Class candidates has become final and would not he disturbed. The Government should have given a fresh considera tion to the appellants for appointment. [130F G] (d) The High Court was in error in holding otherwise. [131A B] (e) The Government had also failed to appreciate the justification for cancellation of the written Part of the recruit ment examina nation and asking for a re holding of it. [132C D, F] 2(i) The appellants were not called for interviews but were finally selected. They could have been avoided if they had been done and the litigation could have be avoided. [133D E; 134A] (ii) The result of the interview was known and upon an inquiry was factually correct. The High court has upheld the actions of the State Public Commis tion and askedfor a fresh interviews of all candidates on its basis.

The appellant filed a suit for possession of the Dera and its properties attached to it. The respondent claimed that he was in possession of certain properties belonging to the D.S.D. as his lawfully appointed mahant. The appellant contended that since the properties belonged to the respondent, the interest which was the subject matter of the suit had devolved upon him. The trial court decreed the suit and dismissed the suit. On appeal, the High Court held that after the death of Som Dass, Shiam Das, as his Chela inherited the sum total of the rights which earlier vested in Som Dass and when a controversy is raised about such rights, then the appellant was bound to bring on record the legal representatives of the deceased within the time prescribed by law. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The suit was for possession and management of the properties appertaining to it by the appellant purporting to be the de facto mahant of the dera. Som Dass died in 13 1970. The property devolved upon his heirs. [490C] 2. The rule is that a representative, the rule has to be applied, the principle that trial of a suit cannot be brought to an end merely because the interest of a party in the subject matters of the litigation has devolved upon another during the pendency of the same suit but that suit may be continued against the person acquiring the interest with leave of the Court. [491D] 3. The principle is that if some of the trustees die or retire during the pending suit, then it is a case of devolution of interest during the penden cy of the suits and the elected persons can be added as parties under Order 22, rule 10 notwithstanding that the period of limitation for impleading them had expired. [489E F] 4. The doctrine of merger is based on the principle of res judicata that in a suit by or against a person in a representative capacity and there is a devolution of the interest during pendency of a proceeding, it is case of succession to interest during that pendency of that suit but the rule is based upon the principle which has been applied. [488F G] 5. The position of law as regards the applicability of Order 22 Rule 3, rule 4 or 4, whether the devolution takes place as a consequence of death or for any other reason, is not in dispute. [486A B] 6. In the instant case, the suit was filed on the basis that the appellant as mahant was validly appointed as mahants and its property devolved on him by virtue of his election as mais of subsequent to the death. The subject matter was the interest in the Subject matter of suit which devolved upon the appellant purported to be his de facto guardian. [487C] 7. In view of the provisions of Order 2, Rule 3 or 4 of Order 23, rule 8, it would not be possible for the respondent to bring the legal representative of the appellant on record.

The petitioners were appointed as Assistant Engineers in the Andhra Pradesh State Electricity Board. They were promoted to the post of Assistant Engineers on October 29, 1979 and were confirmed in that post with effect from October 29. 1979. The Government of Andhra Pradesh by a notification dated October 29 1979 fixed the age of retirement at 58 years for all Government employees including those who had retired from service on or after October 29 1980. In the writ petitions filed before the High Court it was contended that the Government had acted arbitrarily without having regard to factors which were relevant on the fixation of the age to 55, since the employees had acted on the representation made to them in 1979 by increasing the age Of retirement from 55 to 58 years; that the State Government had not acted unreasonably in giving any previous notice to the employees which would have enabled them to arrange their affairs on the eve of retirement; and that the decision of the Government was bad for a total non application of mind to relevant facts and circumstances bearing on the question of fixation of retirement. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court it is contended on behalf of the petitioners that (i) the Government acted arbitrarily in giving no previous notice; (ii) the decision taken by the Government in order to reduce the age was arbitrary or unreasonable and (iii) the State had not given any prior notice to its employees which could have enabled it to arrange them on the reopening of their service. Dismissing the petitions, ^ HELD: 1. The petitioners are entitled to raise the question whether the Government exercised its power arbitrarily without taking into account factors which are relevant on that date. [538B] 2.1 The Government acted unreasonably and in giving a prior notice of its decision to reduce it to 58. It is not open to the Court to go behind the said decision as arbitrary or irrational. [439C D] 2(a) The Government had taken a policy decision to increase the age by increasing it from 55 years to 58, but it was not so in the circumstances of the case. [40E F] (b) It is well settled that the power conferred on the Government by the proviso to Article 309 read with Article 313 cannot be exercised arbitrarily or capriciously. The State has a right to choose between the two classes of employees and the Government can choose between them.

The appellants are dealers in milk and are registered under the Haryana Sales Tax Act, 1973. They were selling their product to various dealers in different parts of the State. The sales tax authorities levied purchase tax on the sale price of the goods sold by them at the rate of Rs. 1,50,000 per annum. The appellants challenged the levy before the High Court contending that the said levy was not justified as it was not a case of sale within the meaning of section 5(1) of the Act and that the tax imposed by section 9(1)(b) should be deemed to have been deleted from the statute. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the words "or despatches the manufactured goods to a place outside the State in any manner otherwise than by way of sale in the course of inter State trade or commerce" in section 9 (1) (b) must be deemed, to have existed in the State and exported them. The present appeals are against the High Courts ' decision upholding the validity of section 9 of the Central Sales Tax (Amendment) Act, 1983. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The words "and despatches" used in clause (a)(ii) later, clause (b), should be construed as including within the definition of 'turnover ' the purchase value of goods liable to tax under section 9, but the goods presently in question are not laible to tax u/s 9(i)(b). [351B] 2. The expression "or" in clause(a) must mean a sale or purchase of goods for the pur pose of export out of the territory of India within the contemplation of sub section (1), but must be construed in its popular sense, that is to say, a sale in one State and a sale of goods in another State. [351C] 3. The word "turnover" has been used in the context of the definition. It includes all sales which are inter state or intra state sales. The definition includes within the ambit of the expression 'turnover of purchase value ' the purchases value of taxable goods liable under section 4, but does not include within its fold any sale price. [352D] 4. The assessees would have to pay tax on their sales made to the purchases effected by them but for a claim for exemption u/S 24(3). They would have had to pay sales tax on such sales to the purchasers effected by they but for claim for a exemption under section 24(1), not being a case where the manufactured product are disposed of only by way o f sale in course of export outside the territory, within the purview of sub s.(1) or section 5 of the C.S.T. Act, 1956. [353E F] 5. The contention that the sales tax is leviable under the Act on goods in question when they are sold by a dealer and, indeed, the assessees would had have to bear tax on them cannot be accepted. [354F G] 6. The fact that the assessees were not registered under section 5 (1 ) or section 6 or section 24 (3) of C.T., Act, does not mean that they are liable to pay purchase value in respect of goods which are sold outside the state. [355B] 7. The question whether a tax is payable under the Central Act on the goods in ques tion when they were sold by dealers and, therefore, the assessee would have paid tax on those sales made by dealers does not arise for consideration. [356C D] 8. The position would be if the assessees had to bear the tax on these sales made in the manner prescribed by section 4 of the Amending Act. They would also have to make a reference to sub s (3), of section 24, inserted with retrospective effect from 27.5.1971, which was not done. [359D] 9.

The appellants who were dealers in oil contracts entered into by them with the respondent State of Bombay for the sale of oil from their factories and sold it to various purchasers. The sales were effected by the respondent company in pursuance of a contract between the parties, and the goods were despatched by the appellants to the buyers on shipment. The respondent company was assessed to purchase tax under section 10(b) of the Act on the ground that these sales were not "despatched outside the State of Madras within the meaning of article 286(1)(b) Of the Constitution. Held, that the words " a registered dealer " in section 10 (b) means a registered person to whom he sells the goods and the purchaser is not a registereddealer. The word " a person" in section 8(b), as used in the Act, includes a registered firm. The words " registered dealer to whom the goods have been sold by him or by a person to which he sells them outside the state of Bombay " mean a registered owner to whom goods have not been sold and who is not registered dealer, are not intended to be used for the purpose of carrying on business in oil seeds. The expression " registered dealers" in the section means a person who has given such certificate under section 8 (b). The words 'registered dealer to which the goods had been sold ' mean a person whose registration has been cancelled and who has been granted a certificate under the Act. The appellants were dealers within the definition of "dealer ". The word ' registered dealer" in this clause means a dealer to whose goods have already been sold but who is registered as a dealer under the Bombay Sales Tax Act, 1948, and includes a person holding or obtaining a certificate from the Collector of Customs under section 9(b).

The respondent, a tenant of the appellant, was married to the appellant on May 15, 1960. The appellant filed an application under section 125 of the Criminal Procedure Code for monthly allowance for maintenance of herself and her child. The Magistrate held that the appellant was a subsisting wife and awarded monthly maintenance of Rs. 400/ for the mother for their subsistence taking due note of the fact that the cost of living in Bombay, where the parties lived, was high, and that the respondent had provided residential accommodation to the appel lant. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the husband that (i) the appellant had ceased to be a subsisting woman; (ii) the consent decree read with section 127(3)(b) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, for a monthly allowance, for the maintenance of her child and (iii) the respondent having provided residential premises to the wife, she was still entitled to an allowance. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The consent decree of 1962 resolved all disputes and settled all claims then available and all claims adjusted, and so no claim for maintenance could survive. [81 D] 2. Section 125(4) of Criminal Proce dure Code, 1973 is manifestly to recognise the substitute maintenance arrangement by lump sum payment organised by the custom of the community or the personal law applicable to the parties. The object of section 127 (3)(a) is manifestlyto recognise the substituted maintenance arrangement as a capitalised substitute for the order under section 127 and not mathematically but fairly, then section 127.(3)(c) subserves the goal and relieves; the obligor not, pro tanto but wholly. [82 E F] 3. The whole scheme of section 125(3) (b) is clearly manifestly to recognize the substitute payment by lump sums organised payment by customary or personal law whose quantum is more or less sufficient to do duty for maintenance allowance. [83 G H] 4. Section 127(1)(b), which provides that a divorced wife shall not be entitled to any maintenance allowance, applies only to a divorced woman who has been divorced by her husband and has obtained a divorce from her husband. The provision in the Explanation (b), however, does not apply where the husband is a minor. [84 E F; 85 A] 5. Section 126(3), (b)(iii) and (iv) are manifestly to indicate that the wife has been separated by mutual consent. There must be a rational relation between the sum so paid and its potential provision as to maintenance. The purpose of the payment is certified by the fulfilment of social obligation not by a ritual exercise rooted in custom. [85 B] 6. Section 128(3). (b). provides that no husband can claim under section 126(1) absolution from this obligation under section125. [86 C D] 7. The respondent having been divorced, his wife and the daughter used to live separately, there is no question of any mutual consent decree being passed in 1962. [87 E F]. 8. Section 12(3A), which is a special provision, does require that the husband should have been separated from his wife by mutual agreement between them. The section does not require that he should be separated from the wife and must be separately treated as a separate category for the purpose of section 12(1). [87 F G] 9. Section 13(3B) is designed to recognise a substitute maintenance arrangements by lump payment organised payment through lump sum payments. It is, therefore, clear that the provision in Explanation (a), which has been enacted to adjust their mutual rights then mutual rights, has been incorporated into the Act with a view to provide for the divorcee and to provide her with wherewithal to maintain herself. [88 E] 10.

The appellant was a bidder for the year 1988. He deposited dak amount in the auction and the bid of the respondent was accepted by the Collector. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the order dated 25th March, 1988 passed by the State Government cancelling the bid. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that there was no requirement in the rule of giving any prior notice before black listing any person. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that there is no requirement specifically giving any notice before the black listing of the proposal of black listing the appellant and that the order directing that the appellant be placed in the black list for future contracts under the orders passed by Collector, Samastipur was therefore placed in that black list. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The rule of law that any order having civil consequence should be passed only after following the principles of natural justice has no application to a black listing. [868C] 2. In so far as the cancellation of the bid is concerned, the respondent is right. But it is an implied principle of the rule that any orders having civil consequences should be pass only after complying with the principles laid down in the rules. The order directing the appellant to be placed immediately in black list in respect of future contracts cannot be sustained in law. [869D] 3. In the premises, that portion of the Order directing that appellant be placing in the Black list in regard of future contract under the Collector is set aside. So far as cancellation of bid of appellant is concerned that is not affected. The direction to the appellant being placed in black List in respect thereof cannot be justified in law and must be held to be illegal. [870D] 4. In view of the matter, the last portion of order directing re black listing was set aside and the appellant was directed to be immediately placed in a black list with effect from the date of his release.

The appellant, a tenant of the respondent landlord, leased out his land to the respondent for a period of 99 years. The lease was renewed from time to time and the premium payable by the respondent was enhanced to Rs.994 p.m. On the expiry of the lease period, the respondent filed an application under section 4 of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease & Rent Control) Act, 1960 for fixation of fair rent in respect of the premises covered by exhibit P 1. The Rent Controller rejected the said application holding that the building on the land leased under exhibit P1 was only a vacant piece of land and not a vacant site. The respondent filed a revision petition before the High Court which allowed the same holding that since the subject matter of the tenancy under exhibit A 1 had also been conveyed to the LIC, the Rent Controller had no jurisdiction to entertain the application for fixation on the ground of title. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: The order of the Rent Control Tribunal is set aside and the case remanded to the Rent controller for a limited purpose to determine what the fair rent of the demised premises should be in accordance with the provisions of the Act. [549B] In the instant case, on a proper construction of the rent control proceedings deciding certain applications before them, the question as to whether the L.I.C. is the owner of the property or not has to be considered by the Rent Tribunal as a collateral issue in deciding certain applica tion before it. The order in the earlier proceedings was to be treated as an order passed totally without jurisdiction, although it had become final as being invalid merely because the question may have had to be consider by the rent tribunals as a counter part of the picture. [550C D] In view of this finding, on proper construction, the High court could not entertain a collateral attack on the validity or correctness of the order of tho Rent Controller deciding certain appli cations before them.

The petitioner, a Veterinary and Animal Husbandry Officer in the Mysore State, was selected for appointment to the post of Veterinary Assistant Surgeon. He was given an opportunity to object to the assignment of his seniority to him in the final integration list. The petitioner challenged the validity of the provisional inter se seniority list on the ground that it was violative of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution. The High Court held that the petitioner had been denied a reasonable opportunity to make a representation against the final inter se list. Allowing the appeal by special leave, HELD: (1) The concession in Shankariah 's case was confined only to the facts of that particular ease. It was not within the province of the Central Government to lay down what are in the principles to be adopted for purposes of equation. If a particular decision is mala fide or arrived at on totally irrelevant and extraneous consideration ations, such a decision can be interfered with by Courts. [828B C] (2) The principle recognised in Shankarsah ' case was not applicable to such a case. It would, therefore, be quite fair to give a person affected an opportunity of making a representation with regard to the particular important points which had to be considered before finalisation. [ 828E F] (3) In order to establish the invalidity of the final list on some grounds of invalidity, those grounds have to be shown to exist. So long as the Central Govern ment has acted properly according to the provisions of the Act, it is not within its province of Courts to lay a down what were in the principle to be applied for purposes Of equation. [829B C; 828A] (4) The petitioner was entitled to an opportunity even against a final seniority list although he was given due opportunity to the object to offer an opportunity. If that was established, the decision of the authorities concerned will have to stand.

The petitioners in these writ petitions are partnership firms carrying on business of import of rough and cut diamonds and cut of export and purchase of diamonds. The petitioners in the writ petitions were granted Additional licences to Export Houses under the Additional Licence category as per para 176 of Import Policy for the period 1978 79 and 1979 80 respectively. The Export Houses had also obtained Additional Licences for a much lesser value under the Import & Export Policy 1988 91. In the meantime, the Central Government issued an order dated April 18, 1985 in exercise of its powers conferred by sub para (10) of para 218 of the Import Policy, 1985 88, whereby additional licences were granted to Export House Houses and Export Houses subject to certain conditions. The petitioner in these petitions are manufacturers of diamond and cut and polished diamonds, which have been specifically banned in the prevailing Import Policy. They filed writ petitions before this Court challenging the validity of sub para(10) on the ground that it discriminates between Export Houses who were issued Additional licences prior to April 1, 1988, on the basis of exports made during 1986 87 and 1989 88, pursuant to and subject to the decision of the Supreme Court in Rajnikant Brothers case. The respondents in these cases contended that sub para.(10) was discriminatory and violative of Article 14 of the Constitution inasmuch as the conditions of eligibility for grant of Additional licences under the Export Policy 1991 91 were quite different from those contained in the Import and Export Policy, 1988 91 and that the petitioners who had been granted Additional Licences on or after April 1.1988, on a true interpretation of sub paragraph (10), should be treated at par with Export Houses which have already been denied the facilities which have not been given to Export houses during 1986 88 and 1989 89. The writ petitions filed by the petitioners were dismissed by this Court in D. navinchandra & Co. case (supra). In these cases, the petitioners had been given Additional licences on or before April 1 1988 under the import policy for the years 1978 79, 1979 80 and 1980 81 respectively. They had also sought additional licences to the extent of 33.33% of their exports made after April l, 1988. The petitions filed in this Court were dismissed as withdrawn by the Union of India. In these writ petition, it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that sub paragraph(10), para 218, which lays down that Additional Licences issued to Export house Houses prior to March 1,1988, and those which have specifically banned under the prevailing import policy, 1985 89, pursuant thereto, are quite different than those contained therein in the Export & Import Policy 198891. On behalf of respondents it was submitted that sub Para (10)(10) is discriminatory and violates Article 14 inasmuch as it discriminately discriminate between Export House houses who were granted additional licences on the grounds of exports during 1986 86 and 1989 87 and that sub paragraphs (10(10)(11) and (12) are quite distinct from those containing in the import Policy 1988 88.

The respondent assessee, a manufacturer of packing material, was manufacturing the same in its factory and was also selling it to various buyers. The goods were delivered at the factory gate on payment of excise duty. The price charged by the assessee for the packing was inclusive of the cost of packing which was the basis of assessable value. The assessee claimed that the cost incurred by it in the packing could be included in the assessable value, and that the value should be included therein. The Assistant Collector rejected the claim holding that the packing material had to be included within the assessable price of the goods for the purpose of excise levy. The Appellate Tribunal held that at the time of removal the goods were not returnable by the buyer, there fore, the value had to he included in its assessable value and that it was not necessary to include the cost in the value of packing as the cost was not includible in the taxable value. On a reference made at the instance of the assessee, the High Court held that the secondary packing which is necessary for putting the excisable article in which it is sold in the wholesale market at the buyer 's factory was the degree of packing where the packing is returnable in nature and is returnable by delivery to the manufacturer. The Revenue appealed to this Court against the order of the Tribunal. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.1 The cost of such packing which has to be added to the price except where the container is of durable nature and returnable to the buyer has to he added to it except where packing is of a durable character and returnable by that buyer to the assessee. [985C] 1.2 In the instant case, the cost price of packing was fixed at the wholesale factory gate and not the manufacturer who supplied the drums and the charges separately. The "cost of such pack ing" incurred by the manufacturer when the packing were supplied by the buyers and not by the manufacturers has to necessarily include in the price, except where it is of the durable kind and returnable nature and that is returnable through the buyer to whom the packing has been supplied. [995D E] 1:3 The " Cost of such Packing" referred in section 4(4)(d)(i) does not in clude within its ambit the cost which is intrinsically and inevitably incidental to placing the manufactured goods on the market. [996B C] Union of India & Ors. vs Bombay Tyre International Ltd., ; , followed.

The appellant was convicted under section 161 I.P.C. and section 5(2) read with section 5 (1)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 for having committed an offence punishable under section 5 of the Act. The prosecution case is that the appellant had a consistent case even from the earliest opportunity that the currency notes found in his possession was the money returned by PW 1. The Trial Court accepted the prosecution evidence and convicted him. The High Court confirmed the conviction. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appel lant that there was no independent evidence regarding the demand, the messenger who had contacted PW 1 at the behest of the appellant, had not been examined, the solitary evidence of PW 2 and 6 and the contemporary records. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The conviction under section 4(1) of 'the Prevention of Corrup tion Act is not attracted on the facts proved. [337C] Dhanvantrai Balwant Desai vs State of Maharashtra, AIR 1964 SC 575, approved. In Dhanvantkumar Balwantrai Desai vs state of Maharashtra AIR 1964SC 575, this Court held that though the conviction under s. 161 IP.c. and s 5(1)(a) of Prevention of Dis tricts Act is to be rebutted and the conviction cannot therefore be sus tained merely by reason of the fact that the explanation offered by the accused is reasonable and probable. [336D E] Dhanwantrai Balwantrai Patel vs State, AIR 1965 SC 575; approved.

The appellant was the founder of a temple. He had been appointed as an ad hoc trustee for the Sansthan and the Sansthan was to manage its affairs in accordance with the customary practice of the Sansthan. The appellant 's appointment was challenged by the respondent on the ground that the Sansthan had not been established as a public trust under section 2(13) of the Bombay Public Trusts Act, 1950. The Charity Commissioner held that the temple was a private property and not a public charitable trust. On appeal the District Judge reversed the decision of the Charity Commissioner. In further appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the Sansthan being a private temple, the appellant could not be said to have been worshipped by an indeterminate body; (ii) the deity installed in the temple had already been succeeded by Guru Govindbuwa and the latter by Balkrishnabuwa, the land had been held in the year 1860 61 in the name of the Devasthan; (iii) the appellant was not a trustee for a public religious trust within the meaning of section 2 (13) and (14) of that Act. HELD: (i). The High Court was right in holding that the deity was a public temple. [527 B] (ii). The evidence on record shows that although Sakharam Maharaj, the founder himself intended that regular Bhajan, Kirtan and worship shall be maintained and annual ceremonies and processions for pilgrimage shall be conducted by the saints in succession nominated by the reigning saint. The evidence of the witnesses clearly showed that the property had always been treated as trust property even by the Saints and the Adhikaris or the Adhikais or their disciples who succeeded one after the other were not owners but as managers of the property. [525 C D] (iii). The mere fact that the appellant had been given a lease for the temple would not lead to the conclusion that the trust was a religious endowment.

The petitioner was detained under the Bombay City Land Revenue Act, 1876 for recovery of arrears of land revenue and by an order dated July 7, 1955, he was directed to be detained in execution of a warrant of arrest issued under section 13 of the Bombay city Land Revenue Code. The petitioner challenged his detention on the ground that it violated article 14 Of the Constitution as it contravened article 21 of the Constitution. Held, that the State law prescribing the procedure for recovery and the recovery of the amount due from an assessee are equally valid and constitutional. The State laws prescribe the procedure to recover arrears of revenue only and they are not, in terms and by themselves, by themselves and by them alone, a territorial classification which is based on an intelligible differentia and the subjection, for the purposes of the recovery, of the certified demand, of each of such classes of defaulters to the same coercive process devised by their own State, on a consideration of local needs, for recovery. The grouping of the income tax defaulters into separate categories or classes into separate classes or classes is certainly a territorial differentia and there can be no question of discrimination in the State laws that vice cannot but be regarded as having crept into section 46(2) so as to provide for the detention of all defaulters for the same period in all cases in all States. The classification made by the State Government under article 13(1) is reasonable and does not offend article 14. The Constitution has provided for a separate machinery for recovery from defaulter persons and the procedure prescribed by the appropriate law of their State for the recovery is different. The class or classes of default in respect of which the certificate of arrest was issued are distinct and separate categories and there is no discrimination between them. The distinction made between the two sets of cases is not a reasonable one but a rational one. The difference between the procedure under section 46 (2) and the one under section 45(1), is that the Collector may issue a warrant for arrest under section 12 of the Act, and yet the ultimate coercive processes for recovery differ in nature and between State and State are distinct. The discrimination made by way of recovery from defaulters is not discriminatory but is based upon an intelligible nexus or differentia which distinguishes persons grouped together from those left out of the grouping.
